subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR DISCONTINUANCE OF METHOD OF MEASURING UNEMPLOYMENT-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of Statistics Canada's press release of today showing the highest number of Canadians unemployed, ever and since many new programs initiated by the government, especially the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), to create jobs are based on a formula which uses Statistics Canada figures, I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald):
That the new method of measuring unemployment which was adopted by Statistics Canada in February, 1976, be discontinued as experience has shown that it is not a more precise method of measurement in that it does not truly reflect the actual rate of unemployment both nationally and regionally, seasonal factors notwithstanding.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR EXPLANATION OF FAILURE TO INTRODUCE BUDGETARY MEASURES-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has not appeared before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs since November last year, and with today's shocking figures revealing that a record number of Canadians are out of work, up 10 per cent over last January, while the minister stalls on the introduction of needed budgetary measures including a tax cut to stimulate the economy and ensure more jobs for Canadians, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke):
That there be an immediate reference on the state of our economy to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, and that the Minister of Finance be required to appear before such committee to explain his lassitude in not introducing a budget that will more effectively grapple with today's economic realities.

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT-LENGTH OF TIME FOR MEASURES TO BECOME EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. With 889,000 Canadians out of work last month, a record figure and up an alarming
89.000	compared to January of last year, and noting that only
70.000	new jobs were created in Canada between January 1976 and January of this year, a fact which indicates that job creation has slowed considerably, will the minister tell the House why he has chosen to delay budgetary measures designed to stimulate job creation, bearing in mind that his last budget missed its job creation targets so badly?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT-LENGTH OF TIME FOR MEASURES TO BECOME EFFECTIVE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have just concluded a series of consultations with the provincial governments on the question of the economic framework for the current year. Those consultations will be taken into account along with studies now under way in the department for the presentation of the budget in an orderly way within the next several months.

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT-LENGTH OF TIME FOR MEASURES TO BECOME EFFECTIVE
speechtext: As it is generally conceded that it takes six to nine months for the economy to feel the effect of a budgetary change, for example we are only now feeling the results of the minister's May 25 budget, and certainly the 889,000 who are out of work are feeling the effect of that budget, will the minister indicate if he agrees that upon the presentation of his next budget, it will take a further six to nine months for relief to be felt from any stimulative measures such as tax cuts which may be included and, if so, is it fair for us to assume that the minister is more concerned with his political timing than the economic realities of today?

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT-LENGTH OF TIME FOR MEASURES TO BECOME EFFECTIVE
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, not at all. I would point out to the hon. member that as of the first of this year there were tax cuts the equivalent of $1,250 million as a result of indexing. Also, there was a cut in the rate of contributions to unemployment insurance which has further increased personal disposable income. The re-institution of indexing family allowances has also added substantially to those incomes, particularly at the lower income scale. On that basis, there has been, effective as of the first of this year, a substantial transfer of funds from the federal government to the private sector tantamount in percentage terms to those brought into effect by President Carter in his recently announced tax proposals.

subsubtopic: MR. BALDWIN-JOINT COMMITTEE ON STATUTORY INSTRUMENTS-REMARK BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which affects the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). I am sorry to detain him, but I think it might be useful for him to stay. It concerns a statement he made to the press last Friday, a question he answered in the House on Friday, and the continuation of those questions yesterday. This involves a statement by the Prime Minister in response to a question by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) on Friday. The Prime Minister said, referring to the Joint Committee on Statutory Instruments:
I do know of the work of this committee and I hope it will report to the House so we are able to study the matter in more depth.
That is referring to the question of freedom of information. I recognize very well that it is not a matter of privilege for the government to make statements which may be inaccurate. If so, we would be up every day. Also, it is not a question of privilege for us to be able to demand that the government take some action. However, I suggest that the sort of statements made by the Prime Minister on Friday, and carried on yesterday, which contain a clear inference that we have a strong, courageous government straining at the leash to bring in a freedom of information bill and is being hampered by the fact that a joint committee of this parliament is failing to do its duty, must be brought to the attention of this House.
Privilege-Mr. Baldwin

subsubtopic: MR. BALDWIN-JOINT COMMITTEE ON STATUTORY INSTRUMENTS-REMARK BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MR. BALDWIN-JOINT COMMITTEE ON STATUTORY INSTRUMENTS-REMARK BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
This is not the first time: if it were, I would be inclined to let it go. I think the right hon. member has to be nailed on this one. I cannot put this matter before Your Honour and the House without a very brief chronicle of the facts leading up to this situation. One year ago this House passed unanimously a motion adopting the report of the committee that there be a freedom of information bill. Nine months ago the then House leader indicated in response to a question that the government was preparing freedom of information legislation and was giving it some priority. Four months ago the government brought in a very wispy statement in the Speech from the Throne with regard to this matter.
On November 15 I asked the House leader what the government was going to do about this particular issue. The hon. gentleman replied that they were going to wait until the joint committee made its report and then they proposed to do something about it. Three days later I rose and pointed out to the minister that the committee could not do anything because it had no terms of reference. The hon. gentleman should have known that, as the Prime Minister should have known it. The committee reference fell to the ground at the end of last session. We have been waiting patiently for four months to have a chance to deal with this issue. The Prime Minister's statement on Friday is a clear indication that either it was a statement made with deliberation, or gross negligence, without the knowledge of what the Prime Minister should have done.

speechtext:
1.	Have any projects been initiated under the five-year strategy for international development co-operation that focus on lower-income developing countries and, if so, what are they?
2.	Are there any indications that such projects have begun to improve the living and working conditions in the countries?
3.	What other major developments now underway, or in the planning stages, are the result of the government's endorsement of the five-year strategy?

speakeroldname: Mr. Fernand E. Leblanc (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT CO-OPERATION-PROJECTS
speechtext:
1. In the fiscal year ending on March 31, 1976, Canada disbursed 334 million dollars to those developing countries with an annual GNP per capita of less than 200 dollars. This represented 65 per cent of the Canadian bilateral aid disbursements. In the period from September 1, 1975 to October 31, 1976, CIDA initiated 9 projects with a total commitment of 176 million dollars to these poorest of the developing countries. The 39 projects were in the following sectors: 10 in agriculture, 10 in transportation, six in potable water, two in small industry development, two in energy, two in forestry, two in telecommunications, two in education, and one each in health, fisheries and topographical mapping.
2.	Yes, according to all the evidence, these projects and each individual one according to its particular objectives, normally contribute directly to the satisfaction of basic individual needs and thus have improved living and working conditions by relieving hunger, providing safe drinking water, increasing the nutritional value of basic foods, providing protective clothing and personal hygiene. Moreover, these projects contribute toward the satisfaction of social needs such as education, public health and community development. Some of these projects contribute indirectly to the improvement of conditions of life and work in disadvantaged countries by providing for the necessary infrastructure for economic development and for equipment essential for production for the satisfaction of individual and collective needs.
3.	In addition to the increased focus on the poorest people described in the answers to (1) and (2) above, the Canadian International Development Agency is currently engaged in various major initiatives, among which are the following: (i) The Agency has embarked upon a programme to identify methods to bring about increased cooperation primarily with middle-income LDC's in the industrial sector. It is expected that the completed preliminary studies, undertaken by consultants on CIDA's behalf in a selected cross-section of recipients, will lead to further more detailed investigation of some of the proposals made by the consultants. At the same time the Agency is about to launch an experimental programme aimed at identifying a broader spectrum of new avenues of co-operation with Latin America countries, such as twinning arrangements between Canadian and Latin American institutions for cooperation in science and technology, (ii) The Canadian International Development Agency had made considerable progress in implementing the policy of untying development loans to suppliers in LDC's with the objective of helping the

LDC's to develop their capacity to respond to the needs of both other LDC's and of themselves. Intensive interdepartmental consultation has taken place as well as consultation with industry representatives, (iii) Working groups in CIDA are well advanced in studying ways to improve both Canada's food aid programme and the Canadian response to disasters in the Third World, the former in conjunction with Treasury Board, the latter within CIDA. It is expected that recommendations will be submitted to the appropriate decision-making authorities in the near future. Apart from the above-mentioned major initiatives, CIDA is also pursuing the implementation of the other points of the strategy.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   LABOUR CONDITIONS LEVEL OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the revelation this morning that the continuing chronic level of unemployment has now reached critical proportions, with 889,000 persons officially unemployed, the highest level since the great depression and the highest level in the history of Statistics Canada.
It is to be noted that as bad as these figures are, they do not include an additional 100,000 unemployed who have withdrawn completely from the labour force in recent months. It should also be noted in this connection that the government has failed to announce any new initiatives to alleviate unemployment and will not do so until its budget which may be as late as June of this year. I submit this constitutes a crisis and an emergency situation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   LABOUR CONDITIONS LEVEL OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
The hon. member has made applications on previous occasions and the Chair has made rulings on previous occasions relating to the suitability of the use of Standing Order 26 in relation to a subject such as unemployment. I have made my position clear on the matter on previous occasions and, in turn, I have referred to precedents which seem to me to be applicable. I do not propose to read the whole of Standing Order 26 because it contains a number of subclauses, but I would draw attention to subclause 16(a) which provides:
The matter proposed for discussion must relate to a genuine emergency, calling for immediate and urgent consideration.
I have said in the past that the matter referred to by the hon. member is one of extreme importance. As the situation becomes more severe, as was made evident by the questions put forward during the question period today and the answers

thereto, it becomes an even more serious matter. However, this does not change its continuing nature or affect its eligibility for inclusion under Standing Order 26. In other words, no matter how important a subject, and while it might well be a proper one for consideration by this House in many other ways-and, indeed, it should be-this is a matter of ongoing concern and therefore is not a proper subject for debate under Standing Order 26.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Laionde (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext:
that Bill C-35, to amend the Old Age Security Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that on April 14 last I tabled in the House of Commons proposals to amend the Old Age Security Act. It is with pride today that I speak on the fruition of those proposals, Bill C-35. The amendments contained in the bill mean that over half a million residents of Canada may eventually gain access to the social security credits they have acquired overseas. They will also ensure greater equity of treatment among old age security pensioners by relating the basic old age security pension more directly to actual participation in Canadian society, and will bring greater consistency between this program and the other components of the Canadian retirement income system which are directly related to it.
I should stress that the proposed amendments will not alter three essential ingredients in the old age security program. Firstly, it is universal and non-contributory, based exclusively on residence in Canada; secondly, the pensions it provides become payable at age 65 at the earliest; and thirdly, it is the building block of the Canadian retirement income system.
The amending legislation improves the program in three important ways. First, it authorizes the inclusion of the OAS program in reciprocal agreements, which is not now the case; second, it proposes one single eligibility criterion instead of the three current ones; and third, it establishes partial pensions, which do not exist at present. In order that the retirement plans of current residents of this country not be jeopardized by the amending legislation, Bill C-35 further provides for a transition period of 40 years before the same, single eligibility requirement applies to everyone.
I should like, first of all, to comment on the OAS proposals and the reciprocal agreements. The amendments would
February 8, 1977

authorize inclusion of the old age security program in international agreements which would make benefits portable to and from countries with which Canada may negotiate agreements. Such agreements would directly benefit a large number of immigrants to this country, especially those who have chosen to retire in Canada to be near their children and grandchildren, many of whom find their foreign pensions frozen at the level at which they were on the day they left their country of origin, and eroded by inflation and devaluation. The central purpose of reciprocal international agreements is to protect migrants who spend portions of their working lives in more than one country. Such people cannot always meet the minimum eligibility requirements of the mandatory social security programs to which they have contributed.
Such countries as France, Italy, the United Kingdom and the United States, from which a large number of Canadian immigrants have come in recent years, have expressed interest in having reciprocal social security agreements with us and in preliminary discussions among officials have formulated proposals involving varying combinations of Canadian programs. Until now Canada has had no adequate response to such proposals since OAS, the building block of our retirement income system, could not be taken to the bargaining table.
The great majority of social security benefits of other countries are tied to participation in the labour force and, in a few cases, to periods of residence in the country concerned. The amount of individual pensions payable by such countries is usually a function of the number of years of contributions or residence which the applicant has accumulated at the time he or she reaches pensionable age.
In addition, most countries place explicit restrictions on the payment of social security benefits outside their national boundaries. Some pay their benefits only to beneficiaries having accumulated a certain minimum period of contributions or residence. Others do not pay them abroad to anyone, or restrict such payments to their own nationals, or do not pay adjustments in their benefits unless they have a social security agreement with the country to which their beneficiaries migrate.
Both the current OAS legislation and Bill C-35 have a restriction of the first type I have mentioned, that is to say, the requirement that the beneficiary must have lived in Canada for a minimum of 10 years after age 18 to receive the pension of Canada, or 20 years before it can be exported. In much the same manner as Canada would want to protect the benefits which as many as half a million of its current residents have acquired abroad, so would other countries wish to provide, through reciprocal agreements, for the easing of restrictions which Canada places on its own benefits, such as the 20-year rule for export of the OAS pension.
Even if the current OAS program could be taken to the bargaining table, it would be unusable in reciprocal agreements because of the "all or nothing" principle embodied in it and the different weight which attaches to the same number of years of residence in Canada. In contrast, the corresponding
Old Age Security Act
programs of other countries yield benefits which are prorated to periods of contributions or residence.
Under international social security agreements of the standard type, the restriction which governments place on the payment of their benefits outside national boundaries is overcome by adding together periods of contributions or residence in each of the contracting states to determine eligibility under the programs of one or both countries. Once eligibility is established, each party to the agreement calculates, under its own rules, its share of the composite benefit payable and pays it direct to the beneficiary. By such techniques, contracting states can make social security benefits portable across their boundaries and thereby protect the social security credits of their residents who work in the other country for part of their lives.
International agreements also provide for the removal of duplicate coverage. Hon. members will be familiar with the difficulties experienced by Canadian residents working in the United States and, conversely, with the situation of United States citizens working in Canada. For the time being, most people in this situation have to contribute both to the Canada Pension Plan and to the United States social security scheme. A reciprocal agreement with the United States government would resolve such anomalies.
I would caution all hon. members that Bill C-35, while it authorizes inclusion of the old age security program in international agreements, will not, in and of itself, give automatic access by residents of Canada to the social security credits acquired in foreign countries. It takes two to negotiate. The precise terms which other countries will be prepared to offer under agreements, and the details of what they will require of Canada in return, will of course become known only when negotiations begin.
For its part, the government of Canada will be prepared to enter into formal negotiations with other interested governments as soon as Bill C-35 becomes law and we can take the OAS program to the bargaining table. I might note in passing that international agreements on social security exclude all income-tested programs. The guaranteed income supplement will therefore never be part of international agreements.
Secondly, I should like to say a few words about the single eligibility requirement which is found in the proposed bill. Forty years hence, the same, single eligibility requirement will apply to every resident of Canada: the OAS pension will be acquired a year at a time, through residence in Canada after age 18, over a maximum 40-year period. Partial pensions will be available for those with less than 40 years' residence based on one-fortieth of a full pension for each year of residence in Canada. A minimum ten years of residence will be required for any pension to be payable in Canada, and a minimum 20 years for it to be payable outside the country.
At present, residents of Canada can qualify for their old age pension at age 65 in one of three ways. First, by living here for a full 40 years after age 18. This produces a pension for which you can apply from anywhere in the world and which is payable anywhere in the world. Secondly, one can qualify by

February 8, 1977
Old Age Security Act
living here without interruption for the ten years immediately preceding application for the pension, normally from age 55 to age 65. This produces a pension payable in Canada for which you must apply from Canada and which becomes exportable after the pensioner has completed 20 years of residence here.
Finally, if an applicant has been absent from the country during the ten years preceding application for the pension, he or she can make up each year of absence by three years of residence between ages 18 and 54. This produces a pension payable in Canada only, unless the applicant can meet the 20-year export rule. The point to bear in mind, however, is that in order to qualify under this "three for one" provision the applicant must live in Canada for a full year before applying for the pension.
Unfortunately, the application of these eligibility criteria frequently results in inequitable treatment of beneficiaries. Let us take the case of someone who was born in Canada, lived and worked here and, say for health reasons, left the country at age 55. The 37 years of residence in Canada after age 18 which such a person had completed would not entitled the applicant to anything unless he or she were to re-establish residence in Canada for a full year before applying for the pension. On the other hand, a non-Canadian, say, again, for health reasons, can choose to come to Canada at age 55, live here until age 65, claim and get a full pension.
It will be clear from the foregoing that the current eligibility criteria, combined with the "all or nothing" principle, can favour applicants having had as little as ten years association with Canada over others who spent most of their working lives here. The amendments which the government has put forward will resolve this anomaly by giving each year of residence in Canada exactly the same value for OAS purposes and by establishing partial pensions. After the transition period, 40 years will draw a full forty-fortieths pension. Twenty years will be worth half as much as a full pension, and ten years a quarter as much.
In preparing the amendments which are now before us, one of the government's concerns was to ensure that no one currently in receipt of the pension, or in the process of building up their entitlement to it, would be affected by the changes in the rules. The OAS target population is composed of current and former residents of Canada. Within this group, those under the age of 25 when Bill C-35 becomes law and who have 40 years ahead of them to build up their entitlement to a forty-fortieths pensions will be governed by the new rules.
Current or former residents of Canada who are 25 and over when Bill C-35 comes into force will have the choice of the most beneficial set of rules when they apply for their OAS pension at age 65. Thus, no one-absolutely no one-who has some claim to an OAS entitlement by virtue of current or former residence in Canada will be deprived of the opportunity to earn a full pension. For the purposes of the act, current residents include those holding a valid immigrant visa when the amendments become law. They, too, could choose which-

ever set of rules is more advantageous to their particular circumstances.
It should be noted, as well, that receipt of a partial OAS pension will give access to the income-tested guaranteed income supplement, as the full pension currently does, and will be adjusted quarterly to the consumer price index, as is the case for the full pension now. Similarly, the younger spouse of an OAS pensioner will continue to be entitled to consideration for the spouses' allowance benefits; the OAS equivalent portion of such benefits will be calculated in the same manner as the OAS pension itself.
People who have never resided in Canada and who do not hold an immigrant visa will henceforth be governed by the new rules and earn their pension a year at a time, as will every other legal resident of Canada. Others-current and former residents of Canada-may qualify for pensions under the new law, while they have no entitlement at all under current legislation, or can receive a partial pension earlier than they could have received a full one.

Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should like to comment on other features of the amending legislation. Bill C-35 also includes an amendment which will exempt family allowance benefits as income for the purpose of calculating entitlement to GIS and spouse's allowances.
When the GIS program was developed in 1966, family allowances were not taxable; consequently, they were not considered part of a GIS applicant's income and had no effect on the amount of the supplement payable. However, when family allowances became taxable in 1974, the benefits automatically counted as part of one's income in calculating eligibility for GIS. Henceforth, family allowances will not be counted as income for calculation of benefits under the guaranteed income supplement or the spouses' allowance programs. Approximately 10,000 pensioners, it is estimated, will benefit from this change.
A number of other amendments have been introduced in the bill to facilitate the proper administration of the program and to prevent abuse of the legislation originally passed by parliament. As an example, the amending legislation will prevent the payment abroad, for more than six months, of OAS benefits to persons who have ceased to reside in Canada and who do not meet the 20-year export rule. Technically, such persons can now defeat the 20-year rule for export of the pension by returning to Canada for one day every six months. Bill C-35 corrects this situation.
Provision is also made in the legislation for the granting of commissioner of oath authority to departmental officers to expedite the administration of certain provisions of the act, notably those relating to proof of marriage.
Finally, in order that parliament may fully exercise its authority over the use of public funds, Bill C-35 describes the procedure to be used for the ratification, by both Houses of Parliament, of reciprocal social security agreements which the government of Canada may negotiate with foreign govern-
February 8, 1977

ments under the authority of the governor-in-council. This ratification procedure is the same as that which applies to income tax agreements with which members of this House are familiar.
Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, Canadians have reason to be proud of the retirement income system which has been built over the years. It can stand comparison with the best in the world. We can be prouder yet when the amendments become law, because there will be more equity in the treatment of OAS beneficiaries, more consistency within the system itself, and the possibility of negotiating international agreements to protect the social security credits of people migrating into and out of Canada.
Let me emphasize that we have taken great care in the phasing in of the new residence requirements. No one in receipt of a pension will have that pension reduced. People under 25, who have 40 years ahead of them before retirement, will have the opportunity to qualify for a 40/40ths pension under the new rules.
Those 25 and over, current or former residents of Canada, will be able to claim their pension at age 65 under the most beneficial set of rules. Current residents, for this purpose, include people holding immigrant visas when the act is enforced.
Older immigrants to our country will earn their pension one year at a time, as will every other resident of Canada.
Pensions (partial and full) will be adjusted quarterly in line with increases in the consumer price index. Partial pensioners will be able to receive the full guaranteed income supplement, if their other income is low enough to qualify them for this. And in the small proportion of cases where there may still be a deficiency in income to meet basic living requirements, the individuals concerned will have access to the income support programs administered by provincial governments and funded jointly by the provinces and the federal government.
We are improving the equity of the program in future years, and relating the basic old age security pension more directly to actual participation in Canadian society. And we must remember that, in doing so, we also make this program more consistent with the programs of other countries, thereby facilitating the negotiation of bilateral agreements covering pensions. This, in turn, should make it possible for many immigrants to improve their retirement income position.
Mr. Speaker, those are the comments I wanted to make in introducing the bill. I thank hon. members for their kind attention.

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say, first, that we on this side of the House consider that the steps the minister has taken are worthy of very serious consideration. The minister, on April 4, 1976, announced the
Old Age Security Act
government's proposed amendments to the Old Age Security Act which would-
-address the inequities which are rising because of the increasing number of persons whose active working life and retirement are not all spent in Canada.
Actually, as has been pointed out by the minister, there were two proposals. One will affect every Canadian through the change in residence rules and, of course, those who recently arrived in Canada, and the other will affect Canadians living abroad and older persons who have come to Canada. With particular reference to the last point, as has been stated by the minister there are some 500,000 people living in Canada who-I will not use the word "neglect" because I do not think it is fair-because of the foot-dragging, and perhaps, procrastination of this government have been denied benefits simply because this government was unable, with all its wisdom-

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext: Wisdom?

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext:
-yes, wisdom and all its support staff, was unable to come up with legislation which would enable it to enter into reciprocal agreements with such countries as the United Kingdom, Italy and France. Therefore, these people have been deprived of benefits. I will not dwell on that too long, but let me say that we on this side of the House take a very dim view of that. I have here much correspondence between the High Commission of the United Kingdom and this government dating back to 1970. Proposals have been submitted. It is now February 8, 1977. The minister smiles. Perhaps he anticipates that I will clap him on the back, but it is not my role to clap ministers on the back for anything, because they are getting paid enough to bring forward legislation sufficiently early to benefit Canadians.
In the last Speech from the Throne we read the government's announced intention to address itself to inequities. There is more to that than residence requirements and reciprocal agreements. I should like to make a few comments on this without speaking at any great length. My colleague, the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Malone), and myself have been out on a quality of life tour to determine the quality of life of our senior citizens, whether they have any grievances, and so forth. Our governments-notice how I say "governments" so as to be purely objective-are doing the right thing with respect to our senior citizens. There are some two million Canadians who are at present entitled to old age security, but because of medical advances and improvement of the quality of life-my life and that of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde)-will live longer in the golden years of their lives. Therefore, we must be concerned about those people because of the attitude of some of us in the country that older people should be shipped out to pasture at the age of 65 to fend for themselves. I heard that comment on many occasions as I travelled from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean and back. There seems to be an attitude in Canada that once you are 65, you are useless; there is no purpose to your life, and therefore you should be institutionalized.

Be kind to me.

speechtext: There is a role for the institution to play, but we should concern ourselves with improving this situation. The reason I am so much in favour of immigrants and immigration to Canada is that the type of person we are bringing here respects and appreciates the worthiness of his elders. You do not find too many new immigrants sending their parents and grandparents to institutions. I see the minister nodding his head in affirmation. We Canadians have been sloppy in this respect.

speechtext: Or worse.

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext:
"Or worse", as the hon. member says. I want to let the minister know that there is concern about that matter. When we talk about inequities, let me point out that senior citizens are concerned about the rising cost of living. We found on our tour that they are concerned about food, clothing, housing and fuel. Yet the cost of living index, as the minister knows, is based on a multiplicity of factors, some of which do not affect senior citizens. So they want us to try to devise a new formula so that the indexing will relate more to their needs.
They were angry about the minister forcing senior citizens into retirement at age 65. The minister knows what I am talking about. His colleague, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), introduced amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act which denied benefits to people after age 65. In other words, this is forced retirement. Under the present Unemployment Insurance Act, after age 65 you cannot pay premiums and you are not entitled to benefits.

speechtext: But you may get your Canada pension benefits without retirement.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when the minister was speaking I did not interrupt him. He says they can get their Canada pension, but I am not talking about the Canada pension. I am talking about the work ethic and those who are aged 65 but do not want to collect the Canada pension because they are still energetic enough and have the strength to work. As I look to my left, and I will not mention names-

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext: Why not?

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext: I think the hon. member knows what I am getting at, Mr. Speaker. If we were to force retirement in this House, some of the greatest parliamentarians would have to vacate the premises.

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext:
Some people over 65 want to work, not because it is a great joy but because they have commitments, and the cost of living is high. Due to this government's ineptness in solving the many problems that are destroying our economy, however, people find it necessary to work in order to help themselves, those they brought into the world, and their children. But the government says that at age 65 they are not
now eligible for unemployment insurance. It has been said they are ripping off the system. Why pick on these people who have contributed so much to the country? Surely it would be easy to find the few in this age group who are ripping off the system compared to the number between, say, age 20 and 25 who are said to be doing the same thing.
This bill is part and parcel of the whole mess in which we find ourselves as a result of this government and, in particular, this minister. The provisions regarding spouse's allowance are also cause for concern and we have fought them tooth and nail. The minister did not have the decency to define "spouse"-he did not even put "married" in the bill. "Spouse" could mean someone with whom you are living. But that is another problem, although it shows the direction in which this government is moving.

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext: Permissive.

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext:
My point is that when one spouse is 65 and the other is between 60 and 64, their costs for housing and the necessities of life keep on and, indeed, sometimes increase. If the one who is age 65 dies, the other one does not collect old age security. If these people live in a senior citizens' home or nursing home, however, the person under 65 does get something, as does the one over 65; but when the one drawing old age security dies, the other one does not collect. Those are just some of the inequities, Mr. Speaker. The provision regarding the spouse's allowance excludes widows, widowers, spinsters, bachelors and divorcees: it encourages living in sin.
The New Horizons program is another matter of concern. The senior citizens to whom I speak are unhappy about the criteria set for projects. I think these criteria come from academics and eggheads who are fortunate enough to work in Ottawa. They are young people who have no idea of the needs of senior citizens. They can only see the obvious, and that is the type of program of which they approve. If it is in any way aesthetic or intangible, they rule that it does not meet the criteria. The criteria of people aged 25 or 30? With all due respect, I think some civil servants should get out of their offices occasionally and see what is going on in the country. Perhaps they would realize that some of the policies they conceive and pass along to ministers are ill-considered. I know they work hard on these things-almost as hard as members of parliament. We are all working together for a common cause.
Senior citizens are also concerned about not being able to live in their own homes. They, naturally, want to stay in the home they saved and suffered to pay for, and live in an environment they know amongst their friends and children. Perhaps there could be some form of incentive offered to keep senior citizens in the homes they now occupy. In the long run it might be even cheaper than building senior citizens' homes, although these are needed too. Perhaps some sort of incentive could be given to children to maintain parents in their homes.

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, these people who have brought Canada to where it is today feel left out of the

February 8, 1977

mainstream of Canadian life in many ways. They believe they have been kicked out to pasture, are forgotten, useless and are not in a position to make any further contribution. I reject that philosophy, but it seems to be the thinking behind many things.
The formula proposed for the residence requirement is better than the present one because it simplifies the eligibility provision. This is a complex bill and worthy of our very serious consideration, so a lot of questions have to be asked, and I hope we will get the answers. As I said before, we are not going to chastise the minister; we will let the bill go to committee so that hon. members will be able to discuss it and understand it thoroughly. There are a few things that concern members on both sides who represent large cities. I hope the publicity concerning the residence amendment will make clear just who will be affected and that those collecting pensions will not suffer any loss of benefits.
I witnessed the government spend about $1 million publicizing the merits of the Anti-Inflation Board, how well it was working and telling us of the impact of wage and price controls on the economy. I hope consideration has been given to bringing information about this bill to the people who will be affected. I have no idea how this can be done, but surely if the government can spend $1 million in an effort to con people about the anti-inflation program and wage and price controls, it can find a few dollars to tell people about amendments to the Old Age Security Act.
At present, to qualify for the old age security pension a person must be 65 years of age and, (a) have resided in Canada for 40 years after the age of 18-that is the 40-year rule; or (b), have resided in Canada for ten consecutive years after age 55-that is the ten-year rule; or (c), if a person has resided less than ten years in Canada after age 55, or if the ten years of residence after age 55 have not been continuous, the difference can be made up at the rate of three years of residence in Canada, accumulated between the age of 18 and 55, for every year missing.
Each person must, also, live in Canada for the year immediately prior to the initial year of benefit, under that old age security rule. Therefore, one must consider the 40-year rule, the 10-year rule, the "three years for one"rule and the "last year of residency rule." All these rules are messy. The situation at present is full of inequities as different years of residence have different weights with regard to OAS. For example, if a person has lived in Canada for 38 years but leaves the year before his OAS benefits begin, he will not qualify for OAS.
Allow me now to allude to the situation of a man now living in Florida who does mind being referred to by name in this House. I brought this chap to the minister's attention. I know the minister reads most of the letters he gets. I think he must have read the letter I sent because it dealt with a matter of some significance. I am referring to the situation of Mr. William Cranston. Mr. Cranston left Canada in 1965. His
Old Age Security Act
period of residence in Canada after age 18 totalled 37 years, 11 months. I now quote from the minister's letter dated January 13, 1977, and signed, apparently, by the minister himself. The minister said in part in his letter:
My officials inform me that Mr. Cranston left Canada in December, 1965. His period of residence in Canada after age 18 totals 37 years, 11 months. Mr. Cranston would not, therefore, qualify for the pension under any of the methods outlined above.
The minister was referring to conditions I put on the record a few minutes ago. Is it not strange that after being a resident of Canada for 37 years, 11 months, Mr. Cranston was not entitled to a pension? I continue quoting from the minister's letter, part of which deals with the legislation before us. He said in part:
This proposal would remove inequities in the "all or nothing" feature of the present legislation under which residents of Canada may be entitled to a full old age security pension after ten years residence in Canada between the ages of 55 and 65-
Unfortunately, even though a person may have lived in this country for 39 years after his eighteenth birthday, under the present law he would not be entitled to a pension. Is this not strange? This bill addresses itself to situations of that kind. We do not know how many people are affected, but we intend to find out. The present arrangement is an "all or nothing" format which often does not give due recognition to the years of productivity and contribution a citizen has given to Canada over his years of residence. In light of this fact, we are now dealing with proposals saying that OAS should become payable in direct proportion to the person's years of residence. One year of residence will earn the person one-fortieth of his OAS pension, with a maximum of 40 years to receive a full pension.
It should be noted that the minimum residence requirement of ten years will be retained, but will refer to any ten years of residence in Canada after age 18. As well, a minimum of 20 years residence will still be required to collect OAS from abroad. Once again, any 20 years of residence after age 18 will qualify. This will essentially solve most, if not all, of the inequity problem which I have discussed. Since each year of residence will receive the same weight, the proposed provision will eliminate the "all or nothing" nature of the present OAS plan and it will become possible to collect a partial pension.
For the benefit of those who subscribe to Hansard, let me put on record the new criteria the minister has proposed under this bill. Although I do not like flattering our ministers, I think we ought to recognize what the minister has done in this instance. I hope I did not sound too flowery.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader

speechtext: In other words, you are not all bad.

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext:
I am not concerned about whether the minister is good or bad; I could not care less, since we intend to sit on the government side of the House. But I want to show our people how this country should be governed in a responsible and responsive fashion for the benefit of Canadians. Let me put on record some questions and answers concerning the proposed legislation to amend the Old Age Security Act. They read as follows:

February 8, 1977
Old Age Security Act
Q. What would the new residence rules be?
A. Under the new rules, the Old Age Security pension would be "earned" by residents of Canada a year at a time, that is, at the rate of one-fortieth of the eventual full pension for each year of residence here after age 18.
Receipt of the pension in Canada would continue to be subject to a minimum residence period of ten years after age 18 and receipt of the pension abroad, to a minimum residence period of 20 years.
40 years of residence after age 18-a full OAS pension, in Canada or abroad; 20 years (or more) of residence after age 18 (but less than 40)-half a pension (or more) in Canada or abroad; ten years of residence after age 18 (but less than 20)-a quarter of a pension (or more, up to nineteen-fortieths) payable in Canada only.
The last part of that answer could create problems-which are not insurmountable, I might add. We ought to let it be known that the intention of this bill is to cut the pensions of the recently arrived. The minister has not said anything; therefore I assume I am right.

speechtext:
I now raise the difficulty of those who arrive here from other countries in their later years of life, say when they are 50 years old or more. Under the newly-proposed legislation, they would receive only a proportion of the maximum possible pension because, apparently, now you must earn your pension. If the immigrants come from a country where social assistance is not available or with which a bilateral agreement has not been negotiated, will their partial pensions be adequate to support them if they have no other means of income? I ask this since I, as a member of parliament concerned about the welfare of Canadians, have some responsibili-
(Mr. Alexander.]
ty in this matter. That is why we must examine this bill carefully in committee to determine if my fears are valid or not.
I ask, will these people entering our country in their later years become burdens on the families which may have brought them over? Will this provision simply increase payments from other forms of social assistance so that the amounts saved from the new legislation will be cancelled out by increases in other payments? This concern was raised especially with regard to the new immigration legislation which will allow the immigration of parents of Canadian citizens or landed immigrants regardless of age.

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext:
I hear an hon. member suggesting that I do not know what I am talking about. Because the minister brought this bill forward so quickly, we have not had the opportunity to consider in depth the provisions of this complicated legislation. The fact that it was brought forward so quickly shows how poor is the government's legislative program. It is not the usual deal where you have a couple of weeks to look into it and have it researched. I was away looking after the interests of our senior citizens. I left last Wednesday. At that time there was no intention of bringing in this bill at this early stage. Back I came, and all hell broke loose. They are bringing in amendments to the Old Age Security Act. I hope the provinces are happy. I hope the consultative machinery which was required has been pursued, and that they believe we are moving in the right direction, particularly when I raised my concern about immigrants.
Here is another question. As I said before, the minister's kit is not bad. However, I want to put some of these questions and answers on the record of Hansard. They are as follows:
Question: Could the amount of a partial pension be increased if the beneficiary resided for additional years in Canada?
Answer: Once in pay, the amount of a pension could not be increased by virtue of additional residence in Canada.
I think people would like to know that.
Question: Once the proposed legislation comes into effect, would persons already in receipt of the full OAS pension, or who subsequently qualify for it under the present rules, be able to take it abroad?
Answer: Yes, If they have resided in Canada for 20 years, after the age of 18, as the present rules require. The same 20-year minimum for export of the pension abroad would be retained under the new rules. In other words, you could export a half-pension under the new rules. Currently, of course, this is not possible since there are no partial pensions.
Question: How are former residents of Canada treated under present rules, and how would the new rules affect them?
Answer: If they have resided here for a full 40 years after age 18, former residents can receive their full pension abroad at age 65. If they have less than 40 years residence in Canada, however, they may qualify under the "three for one" rule-but they have to return to Canada and reside here during the year preceding commencement of the pension. Under the new rules, a former resident of Canada with at least 20 years of prior legal residence here after age 18 would be entitled to receive a portion of the full pension abroad at age 65, without returning to Canada.
February 8, 1977

Question: To whom would the new residence rules apply?
Answer: After a transition period of 40 years, to everybody.
That is something I will have to look into. This is an example where we do not know what the minister is talking about. It seems obvious, but we will have to ask quite a few questions.
During the transition period, however, only to residents of Canada under the age of 25 when the new rules come into force, and to anyone, irrespective of age, who at that time, is not residing in Canada, has not had prior legal residence here after the age of 18, or does not hold an immigrant visa.
Persons 25 and over residing in Canada, having had prior legal residence here after the age of 18 or holding an immigrant visa when the new rules come into force, will have the opportunity, as they have now, to qualify for a full pension under the existing residence requirements. If they cannot qualify for a full pension under the existing rules, they could receive a partial pension related to their years of residence in Canada, under the new rules.
That is the part I am talking about regarding the immigrant.
Question:. Would the new rules affect pensions already in pay?
Answer: The proposed amendments would not affect OAS pensions currently in pay nor would they apply to persons who, when the proposed new rules come into force, are 25 years of age or over and are residents of Canada, have had prior legal residence here after the age of 18, or hold an immigrant visa, unless those persons so elect.
It is with regard to these types of matters that the minister should ensure sufficient publicity is given, because at first blush it is extremely complicated. Let us get into the other matter which of course is of some importance. This question affects some 500,000 people in this country as well as those who intend to come here. It can be generally stated that all countries pay pensions, if available, to all within their own respective territories, but there is a difference if the person begins to reside abroad. We are now getting into the reciprocal agreement matter which I believe is important. It is necessary, and we should ensure that it is implemented as soon as possible. The differences to which I have referred include things such as some pay abroad under certain conditions, and some pay abroad to eligible nationals. For example, Canada and the United Kingdom pay abroad to nationals and aliens, but the United States pays aliens abroad if they are nationals of countries which pay social security benefits abroad in full to beneficiaries who are United States' nationalists. That is important. It will be seen that there are a lot of "if' and "but" approaches to security in terms of who gets what, depending on where you were born and what you contributed before you left the country.
There are problems with regard to increases, particularly as this system applies to those who live in the United Kingdom, France and Italy. Adjustments to Canada old age security, etc., are paid abroad because of our present legislation. The United Kingdom pays such increases abroad only to countries which have reciprocal agreements or arrangements on social security. It is interesting to note that there is such an agreement with the United States and the United Kingdom, but lo and behold, the same, necessary agreement between Canada and the United Kingdom is not yet in effect. That is what we are dealing with now.
Old Age Security Act
Since 1959, the United Kingdom, with the consent of Canada, pays its pensions to persons returning from Canada who have failed the residence test. This is a unilateral arrangement, no obligation being incurred on the Canadian side and it confers no advantage on persons moving from the United Kingdom. If you live in some parts of the United Kingdom, you may get an increase or the possibility of indexing, but once you are here you do not get that. That is what this bill will allow people to acquire, if I understand it correctly.
At present, the United Kingdom feels that the cost of increases falls on contributors and employers in the United Kingdom, and therefore it is unreasonable and unfair to pay such increases to those outside the country. However, this policy can be modified by reciprocal agreements covering matters of the social security of people moving between these two countries and effecting avoidance of dual liability for contributions, the combining of periods of residence and labour force attachment in countries for benefit purposes, and a transfer of benefits of all kinds from one country to another. Under this type of reciprocal agreement, they usually include a provision enabling increases to be paid in either country.
In the meantime, a limited social security agreement exists between the United Kingdom and Canada designed to benefit persons returning to Britain from Canada after substantial periods of residence in Canada who fail to qualify for the Canadian old age security pension. I am using the United Kingdom as an example because I was able to get more information on it than others. The United Kingdom, in an exchange of letters with the Canadian government in 1959, undertook to pay United Kingdom pensions to such persons if they satisfied the same conditions as to age and United Kingdom residence as are applied by the Canadian law in Canada. At present, because of the lack of legislative initiative, Canada is unable to negotiate bilateral agreements involving old age security in order to make pension benefits portable across territories.
The new amendments seek the authority to negotiate such agreements so that credits from the various countries will become collectable. Therefore, on the international level proposals are now being introduced to protect the acquired social security credits of our residents who migrate across international borders during their active years, by negotiating reciprocal agreements with other countries. This would facilitate the receipt of pension credits accumulated by immigrants in their country of origin though they now reside in Canada.
Reciprocal agreements make social security portable between contracting countries and allow for the co-ordination of their social security programs. They will close the gaps in social security coverage. For example, if one country has a retirement plan based on employment, and another country has one based on residence, the person migrating will have problems receiving adequate coverage unless some arrangements are made between the countries to recognize his contributions to both. Therefore, we are going in the right direction; there is no question about that.

February 8, 1977
Old Age Security Act
Another point is that by simple agreement we will remove duplicate social security coverage. Some countries require persons to contribute to their social security programs while in the country, though not resident: for example, the United States. Another point is that we shall be using the procedures of totalizing and prorating in determining an applicant's eligibility for benefit. Totalizing allows periods of residence or contribution in each of the contracting states to be combined for the purpose of determining the person's eligibility in one or both states. As the minister said, periods in country A are considered to be periods in country B as well.
Prorating involves the calculation of the amount of benefits payable by each contracting state in proportion to the periods of residence of contribution in them. Each contracting state is responsible for calculating its portion of the benefit payable under its legislation and for paying its fraction of the composite benefit. I should like to point out that the combination of the new residency requirement and the reciprocal agreements will make the old age security program consistent with the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan. At present those programs are related to actual earnings and are prorated over the time during which a person has contributed. Old age security payments are at present not prorated over the time of Canadian residency. Further, the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan are obtainable from anywhere, whereas old age security benefits can be obtained only after one year of residency immediately prior to the beginning of benefits unless one has lived in Canada for 40 years after the age of 18. I might add that at present the Canada and Quebec pension plans may be included in international social security agreements by legislative authority.
Once the bill before us is proclaimed, the federal government can begin to negotiate agreements with countries such as Italy, the United States and the United Kingdom which have expressed a desire for reciprocal agreements many times in the past. I understand other countries such as Belgium, Bermuda, Guyana, Jamaica, Malta, Norway, France and Turkey would definitely be interested.
In conclusion, I have certain questions and answers which I should like to put on record in Hansard for the edification of my colleagues and people across Canada. These are questions relating to reciprocal agreements which have been both posed and answered by the officials:
Question: Would Canada and Canadian residents be net gainers under such agreements or would the other countries and their residents?
Answer: There can only be a complete answer to this question after we have entered into agreements, since total benefit flows between countries depend upon such factors as the number of beneficiairies who qualify, their age and length of connection to the labour force, the number of immigrants remaining in Canada and the programs included in individual agreements. Because a greater number of people come here to live than leave Canada, the balance of expenditures is likely to be in Canada's favour.
We shall have to look in some depth at that question and the answer given, Mr. Speaker. Here is the other question and answer:
Question: If enacted, will the proposed legislation increase or reduce the total cost of the old age security program?
Answer: The proposed amendments will not alter the cost of the program to any significant degree.
That is a phrase which I do not altogether understand. It depends, I suppose, on what one means by "significant". I know the minister has touched on this aspect, but I want to put these matters on record so we shall know what answer is given at this time and compare it with the answer which might be given in the future when we ask the same question. The answer continues:
As a matter of fact, the amendments may result in a marginal reduction in the total cost of the OAS program after, say, the first ten years of operation. What will happen, however, under reciprocal social security agreements, is that a significant amount of foreign benefits which are not presently payable in Canada will become so.
Mr. Speaker, I have tried to put before the House the import of the legislation and indicate the aspects to which some thought ought to be given. I would hope that the details of the legislation meet the criteria of, in the first instance, Italy, the United States and the United Kingdom, the countries which have been pressing hard for arrangements of this kind. I do not know how we can be sure of this. Possibly our ambassadors abroad keep those countries informed, or perhaps they have already seen the legislation. Are high level discussions carried on between Canadian officials and officials of those countries?
I make these comments in the hope that once this legislation is given royal assent it will not be long before we can put the old "John Henry" on the respective agreements. I hope it will not be a matter of months or years before we can bring these arrangements into operation. Let me emphasize that in the absence of reciprocal agreements immigrants will continue to be deprived of benefits earned in their former countries of residence. Other speakers from my party will touch on these matters in more detail, but you can rest assured, Mr. Speaker, that we will give this bill top priority to see that those who have been denied for so long will at last be given benefits they so richly deserve.

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the things this bill does are good. We shall therefore give it not only our consideration but our support. A sentence like that carries with it the implication that there are some things which the bill fails to do, and before I end my remarks I shall refer to some of those shortcomings and urge the government to give consideration to those matters as well. However, I should first deal with the bill which is before us.
We welcome the proposed changes. As I was listening to the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), I went through two or three cycles of trying to decide what to say to him. At times he annoyed me, but I thought: No, this is not a time to be critical. I finally decided that instead of trying to answer him or attack him for some of the things he said, I would make an appeal to him. My appeal is based on the fact that what is most needed in Canada with respect to this bill is an understanding of it. My appeal to the hon. member and to his colleagues in the Progressive Conservative party is that

February 8, 1977

they join with all of us in the House in helping to explain this measure to the people of Canada, instead of nitpicking at it, as 1 am afraid he did in much of his speech this afternoon.
This is not a bill which has been thrown at us out of the blue. I know it did not get first reading until January 31, which is eight days ago, not three, but I also know that ideas such as those expressed in this legislation were first discussed in the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs some three or four years ago.
I also know that on April 14, 1976, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) made a statement in the House as to the government's intentions, and this bill is practically in line with those intentions. There was also a briefing session a few days ago to which all of us could go. So I suggest that we are not taken by surprise today; we knew what was coming. Furthermore, many of the provisions that are in this bill answer problems and questions that we have raised from time to time. So because what is mainly needed is an explanatory role, I hope that all of us in the House of Commons will join in that role.
1 might take just a moment to say that 1 do smile at a piece of legislation which puts in it a proposal for its maturity not to be reached for 40 years. The suggestion is that somehow the arrangements set in this bill will be there intact for 40 years. Sir, the first old age pension act agreed to by both Houses of Parliament was passed in 1926, and old age pensions under the original regime came into effect in Canada in 1927, just about 50 years ago this very month. I have not taken the trouble to count how many changes we have made in our pension legislation in those 50 years, but I would say it is in the order of 25 to 30 times that we have amended our pension legislation. So I suspect that this new legislation will not stay just as it is for 40 years; there will be lots of changes down the road. I take it from the minister's smile that he takes the same attitude that I take in this regard.

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext: You will still be here then.

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, I was aware of the beginnings of old age pensions. I was aware of the battle that was put up by the former member for Winnipeg North Centre, the late J. S. Woodsworth. I have been here through most of the changes that have been made, so I thank my hon. friend for his invitation that I continue to be a member of this House until this bill has reached its full maturity.
1 have indicated that my general response to this bill is favourable. For, after all, it is, in what it does, a housekeeping matter; it sorts out technical problems rather than changing any policy. Even at the risk of repeating what the minister said, may I indicate some of the things that it does which I think are good. First of all, it solves in a rational way the problem of Canadians who have lived here before they reached the age of 65 and who feel they have some entitlement to a pension from the country they have lived in, even though they
Old Age Security Act
have moved away. At the moment, the rules requiring residence for the last ten years, or coming back for a year, or the "three for one" rule, are indeed complicated, but the new legislation will put it on a very simple basis. Anyone who has been in Canada since the age of 18, no matter when he goes away, will be able to get that many fortieths of the pension that there are years he was here following the age of 18. So it solves that particular problem for many Canadians.
We have all had the experience of hearing about many Canadians who have gone abroad and who would like to get a pension. We write to them and say that there is a way they can do so, but it means coming back to Canada for a certain length of time. This is impossible in some cases, and costly in others, so it is not very practical. This is a practical, sensible way to solve this problem, and we welcome it.
Secondly, it does something for a great many Canadians who are here now, particularly persons who have come here from the United Kingdom. I have noticed the interest with which the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) and the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) have been following this legislation. If the correspondence I get from their constituents is an indication of the correspondence that they get, then they know, as I know, that there are many persons in that part of Canada as well as in other parts who came here from the United Kingdom and other countries who have pensions from those countries which are frozen because there is no basis for a reciprocal agreement respecting pensions between Canada and their country of origin.
Once this bill is passed and the agreements have been drawn up, this particular problem will be solved. People from the United Kingdom and from other countries who are living in Canada and whose pensions from their country of origin are frozen will have their pensions from their homelands escalated, so for them this legislation is good.
It will also do something for many persons in Canada who have come from a number of countries where they earned pension rights that they are not getting at all. Never mind getting a pension on a frozen basis, Mr. Speaker; many of them are not getting a pension at all because they have come to a different land and there is no reciprocal agreement. As the minister said in his introductory remarks, there are probably 500,000 people in these two categories living in Canada who will see an improvement in the amount of the pension they are receiving once this legislation goes through and the reciprocal agreements which are made possible under it are put into effect. This is good, and I think we should say so.
The only persons about whom there is any question as to what is going to happen are those persons not yet here, who do not have visas, and may not even be planning to come. These are people who come here, after this legislation is in effect, at the age of 45, 50, 55, and who will not be able to get, in the space of ten years, the full pension that such persons now here are able to get. What we should say to them, apart from the element of fairness which the minister, I thought, dealt with quite adequately, is that the reciprocal arrangements which are possible mean that these people may well be able to get,

February 8, 1977
Old Age Security Act
when they do come to Canada, a pension that they have earned in their original place of residence-or original places, if they have been in two or three countries-together with a portion of the Canadian old age security pension. In the end, they can probably be just as well off, perhaps even better off. The total amount of pensions they have earned in various countries could well amount to more than the basic old age security pension in this country.
It must also be said with respect to these people, despite the criticisms that I still register against the means test which applies to the guaranteed income supplement, that it is available to them in full. Therefore, the only people who can have any doubts about their being treated fairly under this legislation are, as I say, immigrants who come to Canada after the legislation is in effect, people in the 50 to 55 age bracket. But the fact is that when the whole package is put in place these people can be just as well off as they are now, or even better. Let me emphasize the fact that the legislation makes it very clear that there are no changes for any persons who are in Canada now and who are over 25 years of age. There are no changes for persons who have visas to get here now, or by the time this legislation comes into effect.
Some remarks were made a while ago about public servants. I am getting tired of these attacks that are made on public servants on the floor of this House. If there is one place where we ought to appreciate public servants, Mr. Speaker, it is here, where we know the work that they do for us. As one who raised questions on this kind of thing three or four years ago in the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, I applaud the work that some hard working public servants have obviously done with respect to working out these details. Perhaps the minister would like me to give him all the credit for it, but I am not going to do so. He has to lay down policies. But I suggest that the detailed work done in order to see that there is fairness down the line was work that was done by these public servants.
There was the suggestion that they should get out of their offices and go out into the country and see what things are like. I do not worry about public servants going out of their offices. I wish that more members of the House would talk to old age pensioners and would realize how urgent are their needs-and I will be coming to them a little later when I talk about aspects that are not included in this bill. In any case, I am making it clear, without any question, that in so far as this bill is a housekeeping measure, in so far as it makes certain changes to the structure of the legislation, I think it is good and should have our support.
Yes, we have to take the bill into committee. Yes, we have to ask questions and get them answered, although our questions have been pretty well answered already in the material we have had in the last ten months. This was not thrown at us overnight, and much of the material which has been given to us in the last ten months has been given to us because over the years we have been asking for this kind of thing. So I urge very

strongly that in respect of this piece of legislation we display co-operation amongst the members of the various parties in this House in explaining to the country and to the people concerned that what we are really doing is improving our old age security legislation.
I would like to turn to a few of the details-if I have not already been referring to details-and make a comment or two. I do so because of some of the strange things I have heard in radio and television announcements. It is really startling how they get things twisted. I heard a report one night that there was to be a new rule requiring ten years' residence in Canada before a person can get the old age pension. That rule has been there since the beginning of time. There is nothing new about a ten-year rule. It was always there. I heard references to the 20-year rule in order to take the pension away from Canada. That has been the rule for a long time. It used to be 25 years, but it was reduced to 20 years. As a matter of fact, it used to be that no pension was paid outside of Canada at all, so there is certainly no detraction in that from the rights which are now enjoyed.
Then there is another line I hear from some of these commentators, who know it all once they have heard a newscast or two, to the effect that the new rules are going to be discriminatory and that we are going to have two or three classes of Canadians. Well, one thing has to be said about this bill: it puts everybody on an equal basis whether he was born here and stays, born here and goes away, born here, goes away and comes back, or comes as an immigrant. No matter what the basis is, citizen or not, it puts everyone on the same basis. The amount of basic old age security a person will get at age 65 depends on the number of years that person has resided in the country after age 18. It is far from being discriminatory, in my view, because it puts everyone on an equal basis.
Speaking of these criticisms which are made, like other hon. members in the House I am called sometimes by radio stations for comment. I was called one day a while ago by a hotliner who wanted my views on this new bill. I could tell from the initial questions that the MC of that show wanted critical appraisal, but to his amazement I began to say a few good things about it, before I got to the things which are missing. But he broke in and said "Well, Mr. Knowles, it is obvious that you favour the bill, so may I ask you a question about something else?" If I was not going to attack something brought in by the government of the day, he wanted to change the subject.
