subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext:
Speaking of details,
I warmly welcome-in fact, the minister noted that I applauded him when he was talking about it-the inclusion of clause 7 in this bill. It removes that ridiculous situation under which grandparents, in particular, when receiving the family allowance for grandchildren they might be caring for had that counted as income against their guaranteed income supplement. When I raised this with the minister both in the House and privately, I admitted to him that I did not think there were very many cases, but because it was wrong I contended it should be corrected. I was interested today when he told us that there are about 10,000 such cases. At any rate, I am pleased that this is being corrected.
One detail which bothered me a bit when I was studying the bill line by line and comma by comma was the requirement that only a full year would count toward the number of years against the 40, and that there would be no fractional years. As I thought about that, it struck me that it could be quite unfair for a person at age 65 to have been in the country, say, 31 years and 11 months, when the next person had been here 32 years and 2 days and one gets thirty-one fortieths and the other gets thirty-two fortieths, despite the very slight difference.
I confess that at first thought I would have put it to the minister that there should be some fractionalizing of the years, but then I think I saw the answer to it myself, and I am giving it now so that if it is not right the minister can correct me at some stage. As I see it, there is no compulsion to apply for the pension at the exact time of a person's sixty-fifth birthday. In other words, if at age 65 a person has 34 years and 11 months, he could delay his application for a month until he has the full 35 years and get thirty-five fortieths. Let us go a little closer. If a person has 39 years and 10 or 11 months at age 65, he could wait a month or two and get the full amount.
I do not expect an answer today, but it is the kind of thing we might deal with in committee. I raise this matter mainly to emphasize my contention that what is needed principally with respect to this legislation is a widespread effort to publicize it so that people will understand it, and if what I have said about these full years as against the 40 years is correct, I think there has to be particularly helpful information given to people so that they will not make the mistake of applying a month too soon, when by applying a month later they might have got a pension of a larger size.
I noticed with interest that the guaranteed income supplement and, presumably, assistance under Canada Assistance Plan projects or things related to that will be available to those, when the plan gets into full force, who are here for only 10 or 15 years. I hope that fact will be widely publicized, along with the information about the totalizing of pensions earned in various countries, so that Canadians will realize in the years that lie ahead that in the total picture they are going to do just as well under this plan as they might have done under the old rules, and that many will do a great deal better.
Old Age Security Act
So it all adds up to the fact that many people are going to gain by this legislation. All those Canadians who feel the country has become too cold and that they have to leave it at age 55 or 60 are going to be able to get, if not the full then a partial pension abroad. United Kingdom pensioners and those from other countries who are here and are not getting an escalation of their pensions from back home, will get it here. People here from other countries who have been denied the pensions to which they have contributed and which they have earned in other countries are going to get them if the reciprocal agreements are put into effect. So the total picture, as 1 say, as provided under this legislation is good and I hope we will be prepared to say so and do our best to explain it to the people of this country.
I said at the start that what this bill does is good, and that therefore we support it, but I have to say that I am thoroughly disappointed in the things that it fails to do. For all the speeches the government can make about the improvements that have been made in pensions for the aged in the last 50 years-and it can be quite a story from the original $20 or from the $75 that it was not many years ago to the $141.34 which is the current basic amount-the fact is that the amounts given to our senior citizens still fall far below the poverty lines that are established by many social welfare bodies.
Talking about escalation keeping the pension up to the cost of living is meaningless to those who did not have enough in the first place, and I regret very much that at a time when the government is bringing in an over-all rewriting of the Old Age Security Act it is not at the same time increasing the basic amount of the pension.
I had a motion last Friday in the private members' hour which was talked out-that is the usual course-suggesting $250 for the basic pension, and I had in mind that the other amounts paid under the supplement could be on top of that. That would be a little closer to figures such as those which the Toronto social welfare people proposed not many weeks ago. At any rate, in my view something that ought to be in this bill is an increase in the basic amount of the pension. I know that these are not the best times to call for increases, when there is so much talk about restraint.
On a more personal note, I want to recount what happened to me around Christmas time. I see the public servants whom I was commending a moment ago-some of them, at any ratesitting up in the gallery. What they think is their business, but let me say that I received a Christmas card this year from one who used to sit up in the official gallery at times like this. Obviously, I will not name him, but of all the Christmas cards I received, it was one I particularly enjoyed. To paraphrase it, he said, "Thank you, Stanley, for keeping up the battle for improved social security in a hostile period." That is what it is. It is a difficult time in which to press for and expect to make gains in the old age pension legislation.

February 8, 1977
Old Age Security Act
So many people say that we have done enough for senior citizens, and the government boasts about all the changes that have been made. Despite the hostility of the times, the needs of our senior citizens are still very real, and when we get into committee the minister will find me completely on his side with regard to the housekeeping changes in this bill but he will find me fighting as hard as ever for what I think should be in the bill, namely, a substantial increase in the basic amount.
Also, I wish to express disappointment at the fact that there is nothing in the bill regarding a change in the formula for indexing. It is simply not good enough to have a formula that relates to the general cost of living instead of to the cost of living that applies to senior citizens as such. It is not good enough to have a formula that is always running two, three, four or five months behind. The time when pensioners need an increase in the amount they receive is when the costs are going up, and it does not help them to meet their former costs to get an increase three, four or five months later for the period that lies ahead.
In these days of modern computers, when just about anything can be sorted out, I contend that we should have an indexing system which keeps the levels of pensions on a current basis related to the current cost of living. I would go much further, as I have from the start of this whole question, and contend that pensioners should get their pensions indexed not just in relation to the cost of living but in relation to the standard of living; in relation, shall I say, to the gross national product. If our senior citizens have played their part in helping to make it possible for the country to produce the wealth that it can produce today, and if that process continues to improve after they retire, they should not be condemned just to the level of living at the point of retirement. They should share in the improvements, and I shall be arguing in the committee for improvements in the whole indexing arrangements in the Old Age Security Act.
I have my eye on the clock now and then, Mr. Speaker. I know that my 40 minutes will not be up by five o'clock, but I shall try to complete my remarks by that time so that whoever comes next will know he will have the floor at eight o'clock.
The other thing I have to say-and I will say it as strongly as I was arguing 35 years ago for lowering the age from 70 to 65-is that the time has come to lower the eligible age for old age security and for the Canada Pension Plan to age 60. My friend, the hon. member for Hamilton West, had a good deal to say about the work ethic and about people having the right to work, the right to be involved, and so on. Certainly, we old-timers like my friend, the hon. member for Norfolk-Haldi-mand (Mr. Knowles), myself and a few others around here who are in the category that was described a while ago, want to be involved; but the people I know who are older and who want to be involved are not asking to get back into the rat-race. They want the kind of security that will enable them to get involved in things that are interesting to them, things in which they can make a contribution.
(Mr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre).]
What I am asking for is not compulsory retirement at age 60, not an insistence that everyone must get a pension at that age, but that it should be available to them, and the pensions that should be available are old age security and the Canada Pension Plan. For all the good things that I have said about this bill-because its housekeeping changes are good-I have to be as critical as I can that for all we have said on this matter there is no reference to it in the bill. But you cannot rule me out of order, Mr. Speaker, for talking about something that is not in the bill, because the bill confirms the age of 65 as the minimum age; it confirms the present figure of the basic old age security. But this is the time when both of these features should be changed.
I see my time is almost up; at least it is almost five o'clock. Let me say, however, that in conjunction with the insistence that there be a pension available at the age of 60, the time has come to put that kind of program into place instead of the spouse's allowance. Everything the hon. member for Hamilton West, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) and others of us have said about this when it was before us a year and a half ago is still true, that it is most unfair to discriminate against spinsters, widows, bachelors and widowers, that it is unfair to deny them full benefits on the basis of a marital test. Persons who run into it now cannot understand how parliament ever passed such a law.

speechtext: We tried our best.

speechtext:
The time has come to replace that unfair and discriminatory piece of legislation with what would be fair, namely, old age security and the Canada Pension Plan available on a voluntary basis at age 60 to all those who are out of the labour market.
So the minister will have our support for the bill for the good things that it does in straightening out the rules about old age security, but he will have our continuing campaign for the real improvements that need to be made, and in the main those real improvements are a substantial increase in the basic amounts of the pension and a lowering of the age to 60 for all those who are out of the labour market.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING DOMESTIC AND INDUSTRIAL USE OF SOLAR ENERGY
MEASURE RESPECTING DOMESTIC AND INDUSTRIAL USE OF SOLAR ENERGY
speechtext:
that Bill C-309, respecting the domestic and industrial use of solar energy, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the bill before us today is to focus the attention of the House on the urgency of developing the potential of renewable energy resources and to suggest ways in which this can be achieved. But first let me thank, through you, sir, the leaders of the opposition parties for their permission to have this bill come up for debate today, replacing another bill of mine. May I also thank the government for having indicated its disposition, through the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) and the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Faulkner), to allow this bill to go to committee for further consideration.
When I introduced this bill for the first time in June, 1976, the concept of using the sun to produce power for the immediate benefit of mankind was known only to small groups of Canadians who were intrigued by the idea of harnessing the sun. But now, less than a year later, solar energy has become almost a household word; hardly a week goes by without seeing a newspaper in this country publish an article on the subject. It is clear that Canadians are interested in the solar option and that they are beginning to recognize its advantages as an environmentally safe and clean energy source.
As to the potential of solar energy, a number of estimates have been made. According to page 104 of the report entitled "An Energy Strategy For Canada", issued last year by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, by 1990 renewable resources could supply up to 6 per cent of Canada's primary energy requirements if backed by a vigorous development
Solar Energy
program. According to the Middleton report, also published last year, by the year 2020, close to 20 per cent of Canada's energy needs may be supplied by renewable resources. I believe that decisions taken this year by the government will determine how much of this potential will be realized.
At a time when energy shortages and the exhaustion of non-renewable resources are predicted, these estimates and forecasts tell us that the attention of mankind must turn to the alternative of renewable sources of energy, such as solar energy which includes wind, tidal, biomass and geothermal. For the sake of future generations, solar energy offers an option we must explore and develop to the fullest. By developing the potential offered by the solar option, for example, we may be able to reduce our dependence on nuclear power with its inherent and dangerous problem of the disposal of spent fuel. Reducing our dependence on nuclear power would be an important step, particularly because we know that nuclear power stations are likely to proliferate throughout the world in decades to come.
The development of solar energy is no longer a "pie in the sky" notion. At the present time we have in Canada some 35 houses partially or completely heated by solar energy which incorporate either air or water storage systems. Funds have been invested from both the public and private sector. The federal government, under the auspices of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and through the National Research Council, is currently sponsoring 21 solar-heated buildings, 12 of which utilize water storage. In the private sector, 14 houses have been built, including six which use water storage. These are by no means complete figures, but they show that Canadians already have become actively involved in developing and demonstrating solar energy technology. These efforts, of course, need to be taken a step further.
Bill C-309 proposes the creation of an institute-if you like, an agency-that would pursue a number of tasks aimed at the fullest exploitation of the solar option. The agency which would bring under one roof all responsibilities pertaining to the research and development of solar energy technology, as was done for nuclear energy a few decades ago, would (a) undertake research leading to the development of solar energy technology for domestic and industrial purposes. At present, responsibility for the renewable energy program is divided among the Department of Science and Technology, through the National Research Council, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Department of Fisheries and the Environment, and the Department of Agriculture. Then (b), it would actively stimulate and assist in the establishment of a Canadian industry producing solar energy equipment through programs like the new Enterprise Development Program sponsored by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. There is a good prospect that thousands of new jobs will be created if we undertake the development of solar technology, not only suitable to the Canadian climate but designed for use by developing countries as well. Then (c), it would inform the public about the uses of solar energy and encourage public

February 8, 1977
Solar Energy
participation in energy conservation; and (d), help developing nations interested in developing their own solar technology.
The establishment of an institution of solar application would help to encourage the development and utilization of solar energy in this country and abroad, but we must also take a number of other steps aimed at giving increased momentum to the development of the solar option in Canada. Here are the steps I would urge the federal government to take. First, reallocate energy research and development funds to stimulated the development of renewable resources, because close to 70 per cent of energy research and development funds are currently devoted to nuclear energy and only about 8 per cent to solar energy research.
It is important to note that the United States, in one fiscal year alone, is spending some $280 million for research and development in solar energy. But we must not be content to sit back and let the United States do the work for us. Solar energy technology suited to the Canadian climate is a Canadian concern. The development of a solar industry would create thousands of jobs in this country in years to come as a result of our efforts.
Second, I would urge the government to increase the development, within the research and development, of solar heating systems utilizing crushed stone rather than water storage. This would be less expensive and more within reach of the average home owner. Third, I would urge the government immediately to begin to define rights to light and wind-the legal ownership of the sun-and prepare model legislation which would guarantee the rights of solar consumers and investors. The assurance in law that due access rights to sunlight and wind are safeguarded is what is needed at the present time.
Fourth, I would urge the government to provide in the next budget tax credits for Canadians who retrofit or build new houses which include solar heating or wind energy equipment. Fifth, I would urge the government to establish next summer an employment program for students who have advanced architectural and engineering training to develop innovative uses of solar technology suited to the Canadian climate. Sixth,
I would urge the government to organize yearly a national award competition sponsored by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to stimulate the interest of the private sector in solar energy and to recognize Canadians who make an outstanding contribution to the development and utilization of solar technology in the broadest meaning of the term.
Seventh, I would urge the government to build in the national capital region a solar-heated house affordable by the average Canadian which would demonstrate the viability of solar heating to the millions of visitors who come to Ottawa each year. Eighth, I would urge the government to encourage Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to accelerate its development and demonstration of the mini-utility concept for urban centres. Finally, I would urge the government to participate actively in the International Energy Agency-IEA-in

Paris in efforts to arrive at a solar energy technology which will benefit developing nations.
Because of the nature of our country, any leadership given by the federal government-and here I want to commend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) for introducing in the last budget the exemption from federal sales tax for solar and energy conserving items-must be matched by provincial governments, by hydro commissions, by municipalities, by architects, builders and developers.
The following are recommendations I would urge these other jurisdictions to consider: hydro commissions could introduce hydro rates that would reward the careful consumer. At present, we have the absurd situation whereby the more energy one consumes, the lower the cost charged per kilowatt hour. Further, hydro commissions could make available lower hydro rates to homes which have solar heating systems installed. Provincial governments could follow the example set by the federal government and remove provincial taxes for the sale of solar and energy-conserving equipment. Municipalities could provide, for instance, a ten-year tax reduction on properties where there is a solar heated home. Large municipalities, such as Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver, could pass a bylaw requiring that building plans should be approved according to the basic guidelines of energy conservation. Finally, builders and developers could co-operate in this common venture by designing homes which would have one or more of the following features: orientation with maximum exposure to the sun; optimal window orientation to south and southwest and minimal orientation to the north; insulation according to the highest energy conservation standards; and incorporation of solar heating systems.
Before concluding, may I say that since introducing this bill last June I have been encouraged by the many letters received from Canadians across the country. I am also encouraged by the fact that the government is well disposed to having this bill sent to committee, and to this end I today seek the co-operation of hon. members of this House.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me quote the inscription visitors see at the entrance of the Ark, the solar heated and operated building in Prince Edward Island inaugurated last fall by our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). It reads:
The Ark-an early exploration in weaving together the sun, winds, biology and architecture on behalf of humanity.
What was early exploration yesterday is already practical application today. We are witnessing in Prince Edward Island and across the country the shaping of a new facet in the ancient, many-sided relationship between man and nature for the betterment of mankind and with full respect to the environment.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING DOMESTIC AND INDUSTRIAL USE OF SOLAR ENERGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, may I express my pleasure that Bill C-309 is before the House for debate. The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) is proposing that efforts of the federal government toward the
February 8, 1977

development and application of renewable energy resources be carried out and co-ordinated by one agency, an institute of solar energy application. The job of the institute would be to guide research and development in the solar energy field, to encourage the growth in Canadian industry producing solar energy equipment and parts, and to increase public awareness of the uses of solar energy.
In days gone by this would probably have been considered a unique debate, a debate on the subject of a Canadian use and development of solar energy. As the former parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), said:
Our own time has been caught up with its own ironies. Recent political developments have abruptly fractured the industrialized world's petroleum supply. Gaping cracks have been uncovered in the energy systems of most countries. We have been forced to realize how single-minded was our energy planning.
Rising costs of conventional energy production necessitates an interest in alternative, renewable energy technologies. We must provide the framework to determine which sources, technologies and applications may be appropriate in this country and when and under what conditions they may be technically and economically viable. Principal sources of renewable energy, solar radiation, wind and biomass, as well as waves and thermal gradients must be reviewed to establish in general terms their significance in the Canadian context. The technical characteristics, efficiency, costs and impact, must be delineated as an information base upon which to build an assessment potential.
Canada can claim a world leadership role in the following areas: longer term thermal storage, solar-powered air-conditioning, vertical axis wind generators, honeycomb solar collectors, and appropriate technology for developing countries. This suggests that significant opportunities exist in Canada for industrial development to serve indigenous and foreign markets.
We are aware of the problem and we must decide to do something about it. The potential of new energy technologies, for instance, cannot be neglected. If, as some predict, solar energy will provide about 1 per cent of our total energy supply in 15 years, there could be up to $11 billion for the sectors involved. In the long run, the use of renewable energy resources is inevitable. Studies for the Science Council of Canada indicate that by the year 2000 renewable energy will contribute between 5 per cent and 10 per cent of Canada's energy requirements. If one includes hydroelectricity, which is in itself a renewable resource, this rises to 20 per cent. By 2025 it will probably have increased to some 30 per cent. Our only real choice is whether these technologies will be Canadian or imported. Peter Middleton, for example, in his report entitled "Canada's Renewable Energy Resources: An Assessment of Potential", has calculated that over a 25-year period starting in 1979 the total cost of heating a house with a solar system providing 70 per cent of space heating requirements would only be 13 per cent higher than an all oil-heated home, but some 30 per cent less than a totally electrically heated home.
Solar Energy
His assumption takes into account an annual inflation rate of 5 per cent, mortgage costs, and a 5 per cent annual rise in oil and electricity prices. Considering that oil has risen by 40 per cent in the last two years, his assumptions are conservative and suggest that solar energy may soon cross the threshold of economic competitiveness.
The establishment of the solar energy application act will provide a base from which to cast about for new opportunities to fill a real national need for the technologies and systems that will eventually permit us to enjoy stability and a balance in energy supply. Renewable energies will be an important component of the next cycle of industrial development. Canada has either missed previous opportunities or allowed markets to be served by subsidiaries of multinational corporations primarily headquartered in the United States. We are in a position now to determine how much industrial activity should be located in Canada and to preserve and protect ownership and technological sovereignty.
We must consider that one of our most basic needs and largest undertakings is energy. The objective of current energy policy in the industrialized countries has been characterized as "strength through exhaustion". We must move away from depleting our capital of non-renewable reserves toward devising ways to live off the income of the sustained energy flows from sunshine, wind, the tides and the waves. Canada is not alone in the world. We do not have the expertise developed here, but we have the opportunity to develop it so that those who have been successful in Canada do not find it necessary to import certain of their requirements.
I say this as one who is strongly of the belief that a focal point should be established to encourage and promote the establishment in Canada of an intensive research capability leading to the development of a technology that will permit the use of solar energy for domestic and industrial purposes as a viable alternative to non-renewable resources. I therefore look forward to this bill going to committee.
I would like to conclude by mentioning that the scientific community recognizes the importance of the energy crisis and has set about to make sure that parliamentarians are aware of the scientific facts in this and other important scientific areas. The vehicle for this communication is the Parliamentary and Scientific Committee whose second meeting next Tuesday, February 15, will be dealing in detail with the question of renewable energy resources as it applies to Canada. I urge all hon. members to attend this meeting in order to update their knowledge on this most important question which will so seriously affect all mankind.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING DOMESTIC AND INDUSTRIAL USE OF SOLAR ENERGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the private member's bill standing in the name of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) is commendable in many ways. I hope it will not suffer the fate of most other private members' bills and be talked out. About ten minutes before the hon. member's bill was called this afternoon I decided to look at its subject matter and then, without the opportunity to prepare a speech, decided to speak on it. I have studied alternate forms

February 8, 1977
Solar Energy
of energy and will propose, before my remarks are concluded, that this bill should be sent to committee. I have some things I would like to say about it.
The hon. member named the institute of solar energy application. The hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Maine) went quite a bit further. I do not think there is any reason for our restricting the institute, if that is what it is to be, strictly to solar energy. There is need for a good deal of research into the many other forms of energy which the hon. member for Wellington mentioned. They include tides, thermal, wind and perhaps others that do not come to mind. During the serious storm in Prince Edward county a week ago there was enough wind, if properly applied, to melt all the snow. The winds were 70 kilometres per hour. If that force had been properly harnessed, there would not have been that problem.
I have to ask the hon. member for Davenport: Why a new institute? He listed five or six agencies, I can recall a few that are now involved in looking at solar energy. I have a very strong suspicion that what we are getting into here might be just one more agency, as happened with Information Canada. When Information Canada was formed, it did not in any way reduce the public relations departments of any of the branches of government. In fact, there was just one more branch disseminating information, and not always in the most economical way.
I wonder why we need another institute. We already have the National Research Council. I have dealt with that institution in a number of capacities over the years. For a country as small as Canada, that council is exceptionally intelligent, well formed and capable of doing the job that is needed here. The one thing they frequently do not have is the financial support of the government. The last clause of the hon. member's bill reads:
Nothing in this act shall be construed so as to require an appropriation of public revenue or an expenditure-
This is a matter of the utmost priority, and we should not be afraid of spending some funds on it. If I had the time-and I do not, because some hon. members opposite are anxious to contribute to the debate-I would list all the things the government has spent money on which did not produce anything worth while. Surely, on a matter as important as this, we could spend a fair bit of money. The money that went into the Bonaventure would accomplish a lot with regard to solar energy. I had better not get carried away and list all the things on which the government has wasted money which would have been better spent on this project. Therefore, research without expenditure does not make sense: we should spend money on it.
What exactly does the hon. member for Davenport have in mind with this institute? There are a number of things that it or the National Research Council might do. One is to provide a forum for ideas. In the reading I have done, I have found all kinds of ideas for alternate forms of energy. I was recently at a gathering in the city of Belleville. A gentleman there indicated to me that he had what he felt was the finest idea to produce
[Mr. Ellis.)
solar energy that anyone could think of. He wanted to know whether the government could provide him with some help to develop it. I had to tell him that no agency of government would give him any help to develop that sort of thing. That is perhaps not too bad because in a country of free enterprise it should be incumbent upon an inventor to get his first-off copy ready and ask for a patent.
If the institute suggested by the hon. member, or the National Research Council, were to function properly, this could provide a forum whereby this man could come to Ottawa, Toronto, Montreal, or wherever, to meet people with considerable knowledge in the field. He could discuss his idea in complete confidence. If he had something different, or better, they would assist him to patent it, rather than steal his idea. They could encourage him, or perhaps show him that his idea had been tried before and found wanting. It is very difficult in this day and age to find a brand new idea, one that has not been thought of before. If this institute were funded, it could assist to the production stage, if necessary, of an invention that was worth while.
I was intrigued to read in this morning's Globe and Mail that four Australian physicists claim a solar energy breakthrough. They claim that they can collect over 2'/2 times and deliver 2 times the temperature of the collector plates. That is indeed a remarkable breakthrough. It is something for which anyone interested in solar energy has been looking. In a northern climate such as ours, with the conventional solar plates in a field or on the roof of a house you can collect temperatures of up to 75 degrees to 100 degrees Celsius. However, to produce and deliver heat beyond that point to where it does a reasonable job is not an easy task. That is something these physicists claim they can do; they claim they can deliver heat energy up to 250 degrees Celsius. With that kind of delivery they are capable of generating other forms of energy such as electricity. They could heat major commercial or industrial buildings, as well as residential. With that kind of energy they would be capable of producing enough heat to allow for storage to carry through cloud or non-sun cycles.
Perhaps this institute, or a branch of the National Research Council, might discuss with their colleagues in Australia the method they have come up with. As I have said, it could be a forum for ideas that would ultimately come up with something we could use. The hon. member's bill reads in part:
-encourage and promote the establishment in Canada of an industry producing solar energy equipment and parts.
To a free enterprise Conservative, that sounds a little bit socialistic. I would prefer to think that the institute might bring the material to the design stage, patent it so that returns can be achieved for those who have created the design, and then leave it to private industry to take up the cudgel and do the job I know they can do. There are all kinds of innovative ideas. I recently talked with a firm in Georgia that is producing a black plastic pipe the interior surface of which is over twice the exterior surface. Its unique design permits the retention of the accumulated heat of the water in the pipe at a much greater rate than would a normal plastic pipe. This is
February 8, 1977

something which has not yet been made in Canada but they have been using it to heat swimming pools from California to Florida, and up into the central states as well. It is a development the institute should examine.
The hon. member for Davenport mentioned the problems associated with nuclear energy. I am certainly deeply involved in that subject at the present moment. Nuclear energy has been an accepted alternative to fossil fuel and hydro energy, but the waste disposal problems arising from its use are, of course, tremendous. In recent weeks there has been a furore in the central part of my riding because Atomic Energy of Canada said they wanted to dispose of, or store, depending on which term is used, the waste from the nuclear energy generating plant in Ontario at a point near Mount Moriah in the central part of my constituency. The disturbance caused among the people who live in that area was profound. The scientists who advised such a move say they cannot understand why anyone should be so disturbed. Sitting classically in their laboratories they do not appreciate the concern, the understandable concern, felt by these people-their fear of what nuclear energy can do.
The fact is that this waste has to be stored for between
100.000	and 200,000 years. This is no insignificant period when one reflects that civilization today is in the year 1977 of our Lord, and that we can only look back some 3,000 or 4,000 years before that. When we are talking about 100,000 or
150.000	years we are dealing with a time span far beyond the conception of the average individual.
It is time we began to look into alternative forms of energy. Had we not started in the nuclear energy field we would not be facing these problems today. We would not have built on the waterfront of Lake Ontario a generating plant, 50 miles from Toronto, which, if anything was damaged, could destroy a big chunk of our civilization. These are the fears our people have, and 1 share those fears. I am hoping to pursue this subject in a great deal more depth before I agree, if indeed I have an opportunity to agree or disagree, to the disposal of nuclear waste in Hastings county. I intend to take a good long look at this before I go much further.
There are many other developments taking place. There are the new designs in heat pumps. Now there are heat pumps that go from air to water and from water to air. This ties in with the collection of solar energy and, perhaps, energy from the wind which would give us not only the heat but the cooling we have come to expect in summertime. The same pump would serve for both operations using amounts of energy considerably less than we use now.
I have discussed the problems as I see them. I will sit down now and remind hon. members across the way that this will be the third time this session I have risen in this Chamber and agreed to allow a private member's bill to go through. I want to make that point clearly because it is something which does not happen often. It is a little humorous to find that in one
Solar Energy

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PENSION PAYABLE TO PERSONS 65 YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to thank the minister for bringing in various amendments to Bill C-35. Those amendments are certainly likely to eliminate many shortcomings depriving senior citizens. I dare hope that the minister will continue to bring in amendments to eliminate other shortcomings that also exist for other categories of people under the age of 65.
So it gives me great pleasure, Mr. Speaker, to participate in this debate, as I said earlier, the subject of which is Bill C-35 entitled "an Act to amend the Old Age Security Act" and to make my most sincere contribution to this important question affecting closely a very large number of Canadians.
As some of my colleagues I am convinced in advance that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), who is in charge of the status of women, intends to bring about through the passage of this bill major improvements to the old age security program. Among those improvements are the changes to the provisions dealing with the period of residence in Canada and prorata pension payments. In addition, one can notice, Mr. Speaker, that the bill to amend the Old Age Security Act contains a provision dealing mainly with the inclusion of the old age security program in international agreements dealing with social security.
This provision will allow many people to keep their social security credits if they decide to move to one country rather than another.
I agree in principle with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) who said the following, which I hope you will allow me to quote, Mr. Speaker:
The aim of these amendments is to make the Old Age Security Plan fairer, to ensure coherence among the three levels of the Canadian retirement income system (that is, old age security, the Canada and the Quebec Pension Plans, and private pension plans) and to facilitate international agreements.
There is no doubt that the provisions contained in this bill will bring great advantages to some people since these proposals will first provide more equality among recipients. However, we of the Social Credit Party of Canada would have wished the government to introduce in this bill or at least to reconsider seriously and responsibly the spouse's allowance mentioned in this bill, which was introduced by the Minister of National Health and Welfare on January 31, and to replace it
February 8, 1977

by the payment of old age security pensions to everyone between 60 and 65 who is no longer in the labour force, whatever his marital status or sex. Mr. Speaker, in a study published in the Canadian Review of Sociology and Anthropology of August 1976, we could read on page 321, and I quote:
The decrease in fecundity which has characterized the industrialized world in this century is now causing those countries in general, and Canada in particular, to face a reality with many consequences: An aging population. In Canada, this phenomenon is recent, but it is on the increase, and this tendency will continue indefinitely: The percentage of the population 65 and over could go from 7.6 percent in 1961 to 11.8 percent in 2001. Present mortality rates mean not only that a greater proportion of the population now reaches an advanced age, but also that these people survive longer.
Indeed, people are living longer than ever.
... Moreover, the equality of sexes as concerns mortality means that the greater number of aged people is characterized by an unbalance favouring women: thus, the deficit of old men could reach 700,000 in the year 2001.
And further on, Mr. Speaker:
The financial situation of the elderly is precarious: the government old age pension offers an income of only $1,600 for a single person and $3,000 for a couple, and yet this pension represents the sole income for about half of the men and three-quarters of the women. Finally, we cannot neglect the added burden imposed on the economic life of society by such an increase in the number of older persons.
Mr. Speaker, as we can plainly see the situation in Canada is very alarming. In any case, as the final purpose of our economy is first and foremost to satisfy the needs of the population, we must get down to work and do our best to find new remedies, new ideas, new incentives for our economy to insure the happiness and well being of all Canadians. Once again, we can plainly see that the time has come for us to study more closely not only the whole system of social security as it pertains to underprivileged citizens such as the elderly, but also with regards to families who, even nowadays, especially when we have a hard time making ends meet, must make do with the salary of a single person.
On various occasions in the House, I have suggested to the government, which is introducing this bill today, to increase the old age security pension not only for single persons but for married men. Like many of my colleagues, I have received over the last few years many letters from persons between the ages of 60 and 65 who want me to defend their case before the federal government, which I have done as often as possible, in order to bring pressure to bear on the government to lower to 60 the age requirement for the old age security pension.
If I remember right, this government indeed promised Canadians that as of October 1975, that is 18 months ago, spouses of OAS pensioners would receive benefits between ages 60 and 65. Unfortunately and to my most sincere regret, the government once more did not adhere in any way to their commitment. They simply failed to make everyone eligible for OAS pension at retirement age.
Mr. Speaker, every day there is the realization that pensioners do not have the income needed to live decently. Sometimes they even have to do without the basic necessities of life. To
Old Age Security Act
illustrate, let me refer to the case of married women below 60 who suffered some misfortune and have no source of income. Clearly theirs is not an easy kind of situation.
Here is another example of the alarming circumstances facing elderly persons. Quoting from a letter from one Mr. Tremblay from Quebec City, which appeared in Le Soleil of January 14 last: "As of January 1, 1975, anyone aged 65 or over and living anywhere in Canada can receive the Canadian pension and go on working, except in Quebec."
"Because in La belle province an individual may get his pension provided he stops working. If I earn more than $100 a month, my pension is reduced 50 cents per dollar earned over and above that amount. For the privilege of being a Quebecer, one must therefore pay a tax on one's gains, a tax on one's pension, and suffer a 50 per cent reduction on that pension. What an incentive!" The letter went on: "Such discrimination that would be judged intolerable coming from a private employer or corporation is not any fairer when extended by the government." Mr. Speaker, that reader asks for only one thing, that the Quebec government amend such a restriction in the pensions legislation to give the people one more reason to feel as happy in Quebec as elsewhere in Canada.
This afternoon the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) referred to the war veterans widows who should receive benefits commensurate with their husbands' compensation where the disability pension was below 48 per cent, as suggested by Dr. Hermann in his report. I agree with him that the former-prisoners of war were greatly heartened by the passing of Bill C-92, providing them with some compensation. The government should amend the act so that widows would be paid an amount proportionate to the compensation paid their husbands where the disability pension was below 48 per cent. Because if full compensation starts at 48 per cent, those having 47 per cent disability, a 1 per cent difference, get nothing. This in my view is unfair and should be amended with the utmost priority.
Before concluding, I would like to quote from the Canadian Review of Sociology and Anthropology of August 1976, to which I already referred to: "By the way, what do people do when they go on working after age 65? In the absence of published statistics from the 1971 census on that subject, we resorted to fiscal statistics for 1972 on those who filed an income tax return in 1970: almost 65 per cent of males and 40 per cent of females aged 65 or over. The majority of them are retired civil servants or others; most of those who have no other income than their government pension have not filed any income tax return since this pension is close to the minimum taxable income; next come investors and real estate owners, relatively much more numerous among women than men.
Therefore, it is quite clear that older people depend greatly on government assistance for a living. Still in the same book, one can read a little further: "If we were to accept the reasonable suggestion that the current activity rates after age 65 would be shifted by five years, lowering retirement age from 65 to 60 would result in opening more than 200,000 jobs

February 8, 1977
Old Age Security Act
now occupied by men and 87,000 occupied by women. This work force represented at the 1971 census nearly half of the male unemployed and nearly a third of the female unemployed."
I admit these figures should not be interpreted indiscriminately because the jobs which would become available through this process would be of a special nature, considering that they were held by older people. However, I think it would be in our interest and in the interest of the whole Canadian people to lower retirement age to 60.
As we are all bound to try to improve the programs, I shall venture to make a last remark in this brief speech, which hopefully will be considered very seriously. It is a controversial issue and I am confident that the minister will admit this. I refer to the spouse's allowance under its present form. Since 1972, when I first entered the House of Commons, I have had to deal with various cases in which the retired spouse died less than twelve months before the normal retirement age of the recipient of the spouse's allowance. Thus, the person concerned, apart from the misfortune affecting her, was all of a sudden deprived of any income because the allowance was automatically discontinued. I admit that the related problems were only temporary in some cases. This, of course, depends on what is left to the succession. But there are also cases where the recipient has to call upon provincial welfare. That is why I think we should possibly improve our income security plan while at the same time providing the anticipated basic pension which, in the final analysis, would be a first step towards optional retirement at the age of 60.
Therefore, although I agree that there is some improvement, I want to point out that the minister has just forgotten those Canadian citizens between 60 and 65 who do not have the means or the health to fend for themselves and who are silently suffering the total indifference of this government towards them. I will take the opportunity I have here tonight to say a few words about some cases of flagrant injustice, concerning particularly the widow of a pensioner who retired at 65. The spouse is suddenly without any income after having received a full allowance during a certain time. A veteran whose incapacity has been established at 48 per cent gets a full pension, but if his incapacity is only 1 per cent less, he gets nothing. That is a case of injustice which should be rectified as soon as possible. The situation is the same for all Canadian widows and people 60 to 65 years old who are suddenly deprived of all sources of income when their spouse dies. All these people should receive a pension after an investigation proving that they are eligible for the old age security plan.
If we in the Social Credit Party of Canada continually ask for and request pensions at age 60, it is because we often meet many people who constantly come to grips with this kind of problems peculiar to the elderly, those people between 60 and 65 years.
So, Mr. Speaker, we should not forget that people aged 65 have already given to their country from forty to forty-five years of hard work which were often very difficult. They also contributed to the expansion and development of Canada. We
[Mr. Allard.)
could, therefore, easily compare them to veterans. Our war veterans went overseas to fight for our liberties and our workers stayed here to defend our rights, to clear off the land and win from it the resources necessary for the development of our country.
Given all the automation we have these days, it is not easy for such people to find employment corresponding to their abilities. Therefore, 95 per cent of them are without work and without resources. Unfortunately, under the circumstances they have to go from one office to another and suffer the humiliation of investigations and other red tape before being told that they might receive a few crumbs within the next few months.
This is, Mr. Speaker, the situation of those Canadians aged 60 to 65 who certainly deserve more consideration from a government which boasts of advocating a "just society". If it were still seeking that just society Bill C-35 should have been the ideal opportunity to give justice to the veterans' widows and to all Canadians from 60 to 65 years of age.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I shall address myself only briefly to Bill C-35 because I feel it speaks well for itself.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PENSION PAYABLE TO PERSONS 65 YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PENSION PAYABLE TO PERSONS 65 YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext:
I see the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) is going to behave a little better tonight, Mr. Speaker.
On Friday last we had an opportunity to debate the age old proposal championed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)-a young friend of ours who is not always easy to convince-to lower the age eligibility requirements and increase the benefits of our various pension schemes. On that occasion I outlined some of the reasons why I think Canadians have reason to be rather proud of our record of providing financial assistance to those truly in need of a pension. However, the story does not end with what has been done so far.
Basic inequities have arisen and shall continue to arise, as circumstances change. It is to these problems, therefore, that I believe our social security legislation should be addressed. Bill C-35, proposing some timely amendments to the Old Age Security Act, provides us with an excellent example of how the government wishes to incorporate contemporary needs into a fundamentally sound principle.
Under the present structure, the old age security payment is an "either/or" proposition; either one fulfils the stated age and residency requirements and receives a flat pension, or one does not, in which case he or she receives nothing. The underlying principle is that one's pension should reflect the contribution made to Canadian society during his or her active years.
February 8, 1977

This existing scheme-and I should like to define it in order to prelude what I am going to say afterwards-sets out three ways in which the residency requirement can be attained: (a) by residing in Canada for 40 years after age 18; (b), by residing in. Canada during ten consecutive years from age 55 onward; or (c), by combining elements of each of these whereby any three years in Canada between 18 and 55 can be counted toward each year of absence after 55, provided the applicant resides in Canada during the year before pension payments begin.
In 1951, when the Old Age Security Act was first introduced, these requirements seemed adequate. Today, however, circumstances have changed more drastically than perhaps even the opposition would have dared to imagine at the time. Mobility and migration have become such common phenomena that today we have had to take a new look at the residency requirements of the act.
As I have said, the fundamental principle underlying our pension policy has been to ensure that all citizens enjoy the benefits of their contribution to society during their productive years. What is required today therefore is provision in the application of this principle for the increased mobility of individuals. It is no longer true, or at least as true as in 1951, that people necessarily spend their retirement years in the same country in which they contributed during their productive years. It is this fact of modern day life which is being accounted for in the proposed amendments to old age security legislation which we are debating here.
As a specific example, Mr. Speaker, the minister has pointed out that a large number of people, approximately one half million, are being disadvantaged by the legislation as it now stands. This figure is indeed impressive by itself, but it is nevertheless nothing more than an impersonal statistic. I should like to take this occasion to describe in greater detail the human side of this problem.
I have been corresponding regularly, ever since I was elected to this House two and a half years ago, with a couple from my riding who immigrated to Canada from Great Britain after their retirement-in fact several couples. They are, I believe, representative of the situation as it exists now.
When this particular couple left Britain to be near their family, their pension was frozen at the prevailing rate of the time. Although this, plus their life savings, appeared ample at the time of departure, the rising cost of living and the relative decline of the pound took care of that. Today, this couple receives a combined total of approximately $47 Canadian dollars per month as pension. This obviously is nowhere near enough to sustain an elderly couple-I sometimes wonder how they manage-much less allow them to enjoy their retirement in comfort.
What is the problem then? Why should they be subjected to such abject poverty after having contributed to the general prosperity of their society? And they are from Britain, no less. The reason is that the present legislation does not allow for reciprocal agreements with other countries with respect to the transfer of pension credits across international boundaries. In
Old Age Security Act
the cases of both Canada and Britain, each has followed a common policy of not paying pension increases unconditionally to pensioners living abroad, on the grounds that our social security systems are designed primarily for the people in their respective countries and that benefits are related to the specific social policy and economic conditions of each. When benefit rates increase, the cost of increasing pension payments falls primarily on contributors and employers in the respective countries. Under existing arrangements, therefore, these people could really be required to bear the cost of increases for pensioners who had gone to live permanently in another country. Only through a reciprocal agreement, therefore, whereby each country agrees to pay pension increases to its pensioners living in the other can this position be modified and those affected be helped. Bill C-35 paves the way to do this.
Let me say a word about the provisions of reciprocal arrangements. The case described a moment ago is typical, yet it reveals only one aspect of the various reciprocal arrangements to be encompassed in the legislation. Most basically, the removal of the all or nothing structure of our present pension system, and provision for the transfer of pension credits between countries will, in addition to the situation just described, safeguard the rights of Canadians who emigrate while in the process of acquiring their social security benefits. Effectively, what we shall be doing therefore, is co-ordinating our social security program with those of other countries. This means that current inequities, such as the duplicate social security coverage which is now required of most U.S. and Canadian citizens working in each other's countries, can be eliminated.
Moreover, under the proposed amendments pensioners would be allowed to claim benefits for contributions made to one country's social security program as periods of residence or contributions in the other. This would be done in conjunction with prorating arrangements worked out between Canada and each of the contracting countries, whereby each fraction of benefits payable under the legislation of each country is paid directly to the beneficiary by the particular country. Thus, the mechanism now exists; once it is put in place, hopefully as soon as possible, we can begin to provide all the benefits to which Canadian pensioners and others, most immediately those of Britain, the U.S. and Italy, are entitled.
What we must bear in mind at all times, however, is that we hold a dual obligation to the citizens of this country and, indeed of the world over. Every individual should be allowed to reap the benefits of his work. At the same time, every individual must be protected from supporting others who are not entitled to unearned benefits. In the context of old age security, therefore, we have had to overcome the intervening factor, personal mobility, which has disturbed the delicate balance between these two countervailing responsibilities. Through the arrangements provided for in this legislation, native Canadians and immigrants alike will be able to derive greater pension benefits while, at the same time, the cost to Canadians should not increase significantly.
The exchange of benefits between countries will depend on such factors as the number of beneficiaries from any one country who qualify; their age and extent of their contribution
2856

February 8, 1977
Old Age Security Act
to the labour force; the immigrant population remaining in Canada; and the particular programs included in each of the individual agreements.
Since on balance more people immigrate to Canada than emigrate from here, more expenditures are likely to be paid into Canada than paid from here to other countries. Thus, both requirements are fulfilled and the balance is restored. At any rate, each country helps to look after its own better than in the past.
I congratulate the minister on bringing forward this legislation. I have enjoyed working with him on this long overdue area of progress on behalf of the citizens of Halton and of all Canadians.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PENSION PAYABLE TO PERSONS 65 YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise in this House and talk on this bill; it is a double pleasure, I might say, since when I woke up this morning, I heard an announcement on the CBC saying that we should spend the rest of this day listening to the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez). We have not heard from him, and in that sense this is one of the happier days of my life, but not entirely because of the introduction of the bill we are now debating.
I agree with the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), the lead-off speaker who spoke so capably for the opposition, and with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), that parliament must explain this bill. In its present form the bill is confusing and I hope it will be improved in committee. I hope the staff of the Department of National Health and Welfare will, across the country, explain the jargon in the bill. I hope the constituents of Victoria do not expect a simple country school teacher like myself to understand the meaning of sub-paragraph (c) on the top half of page 13 of the bill which reads:
If the monthly family income of the pensioner and spouse is greater than four thirds of the rounded reduced pension equivalent, the amount remaining, if any, after deducting from the supplement equivalent one dollar for each full four dollars of the residual family income of the pensioner and spouse.
I hope the department can explain that language to people reaching pension age who ask for help.
The history of this bill is peculiar. It came to the attention of parliament last April; at least it was announced last April. One of the enchanting things about being in the House of Commons is that you get a glimpse into matters you do not fully understand. Last April 14 the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) rose on motions to announce that he intended to bring in the bill in a few months. I sat there rather open-mouthed, wondering why it was necessary to make a statement that day, and I still wonder why the minister did it. Perhaps, after the next election, the minister will write his memoirs and we shall then find out what he really intended to announce on April 14 and why, instead, he announced that he would introduce this bill in a few months.
This bill is in two main parts. One part deals with partial pensions, which are an innovation in Canada and I suppose almost everywhere else in the world. I have not before heard of partial pensions, but they are dealt with in the first part of the bill about which I want to speak. The second part of the bill

has to do with reciprocal pension agreements with other countries.
I shall now deal with the first part of the bill, that part to do with partial pensions. Let no one think that this is not an important piece of legislation so far as pensions are concerned, because it certainly is. The rules and regulations set out under this bill will do much to discourage immigrants to Canada from expecting pension benefits. As is well known, at present people coming to Canada can qualify in ten years for a full pension. Under the new provision, one year's residence in this country will entitle you to one fortieth of the full pension. Let me illustrate what this provision will mean. According to my understanding of the bill, if a person at age 26 were to come to Canada and work here for the next 39 years, he still would not be entitled to a full pension at age 65. Compare that situation with the present situation. Clearly, there will be a substantial saving to the treasury and a corresponding substantial loss of benefits to those people who will have lived in Canada for 25 or 35 years before reaching retirement age.
The other point I wish to raise has to do with what happens if you can only draw about a quarter of a pension. You must have lived here ten years in order to draw ten fortieths of the full pension. That means that if you came here at age 55 and began drawing your pension at age 65, under present arrangements you would get a pension of about $35 a month. I cannot understand the philosophy behind the provision of the bill which says that from then on, no matter how much longer you reside in Canada, your pension will not increase, that is, your basic pension will not increase as you get older and spend more time in Canada.
Of course you will get the indexing increase, but on a prorata basis. This means that you will not get the same money increase as the person drawing the full pension. You will get about one quarter of the increase, to cope with the cost of living. It will be extremely difficult for people on partial pensions to keep up with the cost of living. The cost of living has gone up appreciably, and, God knows, the supplement or the indexing does not pay for that much of the increase. However, for a person who will only be getting one quarter of the indexing, it will be a very difficult time as he or she gets older.
A part of this system that was not mentioned by the minister will be the difficulty of choice for those coming here in late middle life. Take the case of a person who came to Canada at age 58, someone who had three years' residence in Canada previously. At age 65 he will have seven years plus the previous three. He will be entitled to $35 a month if he opts, and he will have a choice, to take the partial pension. The choice is that he could wait until age 98 and get a full pension. I doubt whether many people would wait the additional 34 years to get a full pension. They would almost inevitably be driven to accepting the partial pension. This ensures they will remain poverty stricken for the rest of their lives unless they have a private income.
No one can say this is a simple little act to help some people and not hurt anyone. It will make old age very difficult for
February 8, 1977

some of these people. They will face an extremely difficult choice. I hope the Department of National Health and Welfare ensures that there are proper counsellors in branch offices across the country who will be able to talk to these people at age 65 wanting to know whether they should opt for the new plan and take a partial pension or hang in there and build up a few more years of pensionable time. They will have to estimate their longevity versus their present needs, which is not a particularly pleasant prospect at that age.
With regard to reciprocal pensions, it is very strange, and I am sure the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) agrees, and probably the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that in all the correspondence and in all the answers the minister gave with regard to why Canada and the United Kingdom could not have reciprocal pensions, we were given the impression on each and every occasion that the United Kingdom was holding up the passage of reciprocal pension legislation. When we wrote to the United Kingdom to ask why they were holding up the legislation, they said that Canada was holding it up. The bill before us, which puts us in a position to have a reciprocal agreement, gives the lie to the previous letters we have had on this subject. Indeed, it was Canada holding up the arrangements, and not the United Kingdom.
On page four of the minister's explanation of partial pensions and other matters, as pointed out by the hon. member for Hamilton West, there is a question. The minister supplied an information sheet, much of which consisted of questions and answers. I very much appreciate having it. It goes a long way toward answering some of our questions, but not all. In trying to determine whether reciprocal agreements will mesh with our partial pensions, we are left trying to find an answer. A question and answer on page four confuses me. It reads:
Question: What is meant by totalizing and prorating and how do they work? Answer: Totalizing is the combining together of periods of residence or contributions in each of the contracting states for the purpose of determining eligibility in one or both of them. In other words, periods of residence or contributions in each contracting state are considered as periods of residence or contributions in the other.
We go down to question 20 which reads as follows:
Question: Under an agreement, could totalizing and prorating be applied to an OAS pension earned under the new rules?
Answer: Yes. The ten and 20-year minimum could be satisfied under an agreement, each country paying its share of benefit under its own rules. For example:
(i) One year of residence in Canada after age 18 plus nine years of residence or contributions in the other country = 1 /40th of an OAS pension payable in Canada.
This rather puzzles me. I think what is meant is that one fortieth of the old age security pension payable in Canada means payable by Canada and that another nine fortieths of the pension will be payable by the other country but payable in Canada, although it does not say so.
I am puzzled by that part of the answer that speaks of the ten and 20 year part of the minimum being satisfied under the agreement. How about the 40 year minimum a person will
Old Age Security Act
need for the full pension? That is a noticeable omission which I hope the minister will clear up in the near future. The other part of the example in the answer reads:
(ii) Fifteen years of residence in Canada after age 18 plus five years of residence or contributions in the other country = 15/40ths of an OAS pension payable abroad.
It would appear that 15 years in Canada plus five years overseas, in this case the five years does not count as far as the pension is concerned. I hope the minister will be able to clarify whether 18 years in Italy, if we have an agreement with them at that time, plus two in Canada will give a person 20 years, or whether 36 years in Italy plus four in Canada equals 40 years and a full pension.
There are some other general matters which leave me somewhat curious. The 20 year requirement of residence in Canada before drawing pensions in other lands is a little difficult to understand. This will certainly be a telling factor in areas such as my own constituency which tends to attract old age pensioners. They spend the autumn of their lives in a salubrious climate such as we have in Victoria. Some like to go south to places such as Arizona in early spring. It would make a great deal of difference whether they have 20 years of living in Canada to count. If they do not have that, and if they subsist on their pension, I expect they will be required to remain in Canada throughout the entire calendar year for the rest of their lives.
The minister saw fit to introduce something in this bill with regard to spouses. I thought that if he could avoid it, he would never mention the subject again. There is a clause in this bill that refers to spouses in the context of family allowances. I wish to put on record once more what I consider to be the meanness of the former legislation brought in by the minister, which is not changed by this bill. It had the provision that a person at age 65 drawing a pension could, subject to a means test, draw a pension for a spouse under 65, but over age 60. The couple having two pensions could get by. However, if the older one died, the minister decreed that the widow or the widower would need no income at all. He or she would be able to live on nothing. When asked about this in the House, his unkind words were that they could always go on welfare. I have always considered that to be one of the meanest pieces of legislation, with the possible exception of one brought in by Veterans Affairs denying prisoner of war pension gratuities to World War I prisoners of war while paying them to those of World War II. I hope those two will both be changed. They represent a very black blot on the record of the government.
There is a question to which I would like to get an answer. I would appreciate if the minister could nod his head. Will the guaranteed income supplement apply in full to partial pension recipients? Can those persons not get any of the guaranteed income supplement or can they get it prorated to the amount of the partial pension they receive?

Where a motion for the consideration of the House of Commons or Senate is filed as provided in subsection (2) with respect to a particular order referred to in subsection (1), that House shall, not later than the sixth sitting day of that House following the filing of the motion, in accordance with the rules of that House, unless a motion to a like effect has earlier been taken up and considered in the other House, take up and consider the motion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the measure which has been introduced today for second reading has evinced a wide measure of agreement. It is clear there is a broad measure of support for it in the House and I hope it will receive speedy passage.
I have only a few observations to make by way of general reflections on the bill and the changes it will mean in the administration of a program which had its beginnings in 1951 with the Old Age Security Act. In that year the residence requirements were very simple-20 years prior to retirement. There was no citizenship requirement. It was a very simple piece of legislation, one of a family of measures which Dr. George Davidson, then deputy minister of welfare, used to call universal benefits. Over the years, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has said, there have been a number of changes in the act. He went on to say that over a 40-year period, further changes must be anticipated. Consider the residence provisions alone. I believe that attached to the initial requirement for 20 years was a provision for make-up of periods of absence on a two to one basis.
In 1957, the government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) reduced the period of residence qualification to ten years, again with a two for one make-up provision and the requirement that the year immediately preceding 65 must have been spent in Canada. The two for one provision proved to be excessively generous, and a three for one provision was subsequently introduced.
The residency requirement survived for a number of years- ten years prior to the age of 65, or one year immediately prior to 65 with make-up on a three for one basis. One further feature was introduced. Residence of 40 years would in any case permit an applicant to receive the pension and waived the "immediate preceding year" requirement prior to 65.
