Mr. Speaker, we now see a change in the bill for good and sufficient reasons. Instead of those provisions we are moving to a year by year build up of residence, with a 40-year maximum over a period of time for full benefit.
The minister, in a clear and able statement to the House, and also in a statement he made on April 14 of last year, set out the intention of the government, and those proposals received broad support. What has happened is this: our legislation has been under increasing pressure as a result of the changing composition of Canada, the result of immigration, and of the employment of Canadians abroad during which periods they are subject to the social security legislation of other jurisdictions. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said the bill needed a good deal of explanation to make sure it is not misconstrued. That is true. I cannot but feel that the changes will be to the advantage of those newcomers who have come from countries with mature jurisdictions in social legislation. However, those who chose Canada and who come from countries without comparable standards of social legisla-
February 8, 1977

tion will not be able to take advantage of provisions for reciprocal arrangements which are made possible by the bill.
The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) said there would be a number of newcomers to Canada, fathers and mothers who came in their late years, and who cannot now look forward to building up full pensions. This means that many of them will be seeking the benefit of future welfare programs in later years.
The changes in the bill will have an influence on the administration in another sense. Residence for each year will count now, instead of general proof of residence, such as was acceptable up to now. These changes will mean that much stricter proof of residence on a year-by-year basis will be required in relation to old age pension benefits.
1 think another change in the bill now before us must inevitably raise another question which I am sure the minister will have to consider before too long. I refer to the relationship of the program as it is now put before us to the Canada Pension Plan. It seems to me that the justification for the continued existence of the two programs becomes more and more questionable when they require individual proof of residence in one case and contributions on a year-by-year basis in the other. Under the Canada Pension Plan, individual records must be kept, and thanks to modern computers this is possible.
It seems to me that the minister should consider a combination of old age security and the Canada Pension Plan benefit so that we have in Canada one combined administration, one set of cheques to be issued, one set of records to be kept. At the time the Canada Pension Plan was adopted, many of us felt that Canada had sufficient leverage with the Canada Pension Plan to bargain with jurisdictions in other parts of the world that had refused to extend reciprocal privileges to those who had left their original homelands and come to Canada.
I realize that making old age security relate to individual years of contributions, in the way the present bill proposes, does extend the bargaining position of the Government of Canada. But it seems to me that we have moved a considerable way from the original concept of a universal benefit, with the simplest possible test of eligibility, a type of benefit that Canada has pioneered. Such benefits included family allowances, old age security and the rest.
We are now being forced to recognize that in the interdependent world in which our citizens move our systems must be adapted to the systems of other countries, and in particular must be more closely related to those social insurance programs that exist in western Europe. These are, Mr. Speaker, the facts of life.
Every speaker who has preceded me has pointed out that the bill has been in response to a number of cases of hardship brought to the attention of members of the House. The government does not seek by this bill to incur a smaller burden of social welfare payments, a smaller burden of social security payments. The total charge to the treasury is going to be about
Old Age Security Act
the same even after maturity of the program, but a great deal more equity is brought into the picture. For this reason, Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to support the bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with pleasure to take part in this debate. I want to thank the minister for having finally brought down some legislation for which we have long waited. I wish to comment on only three aspects of the bill, and on the first one I shall be short.
The hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis), who preceded me, mentioned the requirement of residence on a year-by-year basis. I think this is good and enables one to build up a yearly entitlement to the pension, whether it be two fortieths, three fortieths, four fortieths and so on. This involves residence.
As a former member of the Canadian foreign service, many years of a foreign service officer's life and the lives of other members of the foreign service are not spent in Canada. For some purposes-for example, income tax purposes-these years are counted as years of residence in Canada even though one is serving abroad. I am satisfied in my own mind that it is not the intention of this bill to exclude these particular members of our society and to disentitle them during the years they are serving abroad, but I do want to be absolutely clear beyond equivocation. If necessary, we will take this particular bill to court if we are not sure that a Canadian member of the foreign service who serves abroad for one, two or three years will have his service abroad counted as residence in Canada for pension purposes.
I hope that the minister or his staff will have made note of this point. If there is any possibility of those persons being excluded-I do not think there is, but if they could be excluded-then I think appropriate amendments should be brought forward so as to ensure they are recognized as residents of this country during the time they are serving abroad. They are serving Canada. They are residents of Canada for most purposes, but for some purposes they could be considered as non-residents. Whether these people are members of the Department of External Affairs, Manpower and Immigration, Trade and Commerce, the RCMP, CIDA or whatever service, we want to be absolutely sure that they get their full entitlement when the time comes.
As so many members have thus far said, one of the preoccupations of a member of the House is with immigrant families who come to this country to join their children who, as young folk, came to make their livelihoods in Canada. They come here to share their last years with their families and their grandchildren. Those who came from Britain have been in an unenviable position. British pensioners in Canada are what I would call an endangered species because of the deterioration in the value of the pensions that they are able to draw from Britain. Many of them have not been able to qualify for a pension yet in Canada, and I am delighted that they are going to be able to do so under this new legislation. I for one am certainly not going to delay the passage of this bill, because the sooner these people enjoy that to which they are entitled

February 8, 1977
Old Age Security Act
under this legislation and under any reciprocal agreement that is made, the better.
The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook) cited the case of two couples with whom he has been in correspondence for a couple of years. I have been in correspondence with something in the order of 200 families of this sort who have written to me about their plight. I should like to cite a couple of examples of immigrants who came to this country at differing times. As has been said so often, but bears repeating, immigrants from Britain to this country draw the pension to which they were entitled on the date they left Britain. If they happen to go back for a prolonged visit of two or three months, they will enjoy the incremental benefits that have accrued to their pension during their absence; but as soon as they return to Canada to resume their landed immigrant status or their status as Canadian citizens, they go back to their original pension.
I know one lady who contributed toward her pension from 1918 to 1956. Then at the age of 63 she emigrated to Canada. At that time her pension was valued at three pounds, seven shillings and six pence, which today I suppose would be valued at three pounds and so many pence. I have made the calculation and it comes out to 13 pounds 50 pence a month which, at present sterling value, is $21.60 a month. That is the value of the pension to which that particular individual contributed from 1918 to 1956.
A couple came to this country in 1970, and a pension to the two of them stood at eight pounds 20 pence a week, or 32 pounds 80 pence per month, which works out to $52.48 per month. That was when I received a letter from them late in the fall. If that couple had stayed in their country, their pension would have been worth 22 pounds. It would have gone from eight pounds 20 pence in 1970 to 22 pounds on the basis of increments granted since that time. But they do not get that 22 pounds, they are getting only 8 pounds 20 pence, or $52.48 per month for the two of them.
Of course we also have to remember that there has been a considerable drop in the value of the pound over that period. For example, in 1970 the value of the pound stood at $2.40 Canadian. In 1976-77 it stands at about $1.60. Not only has the value of the pound dropped, but in terms of purchasing power the value of the dollar has also been considerably eroded, so that while $52.48 might have sounded pretty good in 1970, it does not mean very much today. Therefore the dual, triple or quadruple erosion of the value of those pensions has eaten considerably into the ability of those immigrants to live comfortably or to be supported by those whom they came to join.
My first intervention in this Chamber on this matter occurred almost on the first anniversary of my election to this House. In fact it was one day after that anniversary, on October 31, 1973.1 had written many letters to the minister at about that time, and I was told that there were problems in concluding reciprocal agreements with Great Britain. Like my colleague, the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon), I

was assured that the fault was on the side of Britain. When I wrote to Britain I got the same sort of answer, that the fault was on the side of Canada.
At one stage I learned that the British had submitted terms of an agreement. Unfortunately I could not get from the Canadian side any response to those terms either positive, negative or neutral. When I was in London a year later, in 1974, on a mission for the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization in December of that year, I took it upon myself to recruit the assistance of a number of members of the British House of Commons. I recruited their assistance in order to get them to push this matter from their side, and I have been in continuous correspondence with these members ever since. I think my last letter to them was written this week.
In April of 1976, two and one half years after the original intervention I made in October of 1973, the minister announced his intention to introduce enabling legislation. Why enabling legislation? I was told in correspondence and in conversations I had with the minister that there was an incompatability between the social assistance programs in Britain and the social assistance programs on this side with regard to pensions for the elderly which was difficult to reconcile and which made it difficult to reach an agreement. I hope that this legislation, which in general terms is described as enabling legislation, will enable this government to reach a quick agreement with the British authorities in this connection.
There is a question in my mind which I would like to put on the record. Assuming that a reciprocal agreement with Britain is reached-and I hope it is soon-and assuming that the prorating formula applies, I would like to use the example of a British subject who has been resident here since 1963. What happens to that individual? We know what he was getting from Britain in 1963. I put that on the record just a few minutes ago. It was something in the order of three pounds a week, or $21 per month. He has 14 years' residence. Let us assume that we conclude an agreement this year and that it can be applied. He would therefore be entitled to 14/40 of the pension, if he reaches the age of 65 this year. That is clear; there is no problem there. However, what about the increments? What about that portion of the pension to which he is entitled as a result of his residence in Britain? Does he get those increments? Is this what the negotiations are going to be about? Will the government be able to negotiate into an agreement the increments which are due this particular pensioner so that he will get his full updated entitlement? This we do not know. We know simply that this legislation is intended to be enabling legislation.
There is still a mystery: why is this legislation necessary? How does it change the compatability or incompatability of the British pension and the Canadian pension formula in such a way as to enable these reciprocal agreements to be concluded? I am bound to say that I am a little suspicious that it is simply a delaying tactic, and I sincerely trust that the agreements will now be reached. I can assure the House that the government will be pressed from many quarters to conclude these reciprocal agreements. The government claims that this
February 8, 1977

legislation enables it to do so. I cannot see what prevented it from doing so in the past. In any event, it was unable to do so. Now the. government claims it can. All right, let the government get on with it. I am not at all clear as to how this legislation reduces or eradicates the incompatibilities which it is claimed existed at an earlier time. I am therefore just a trifle skeptical, because the government has given me very little cause to be otherwise. However, I hope I am wrong.
I have spoken about the need to include in the legislation, if it is not already fully and adequately covered-and legally covered so that a court will uphold it-provision for Canadians who are serving abroad in Canada's foreign service. I have covered the need for an early conclusion of agreements. The third matter I wanted to talk about was the consumer price index as it applies to pensions.
As was mentioned this afternoon in the opening statement by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), one of the things we discovered on our tour-and I accompanied the hon. member on part of his tour with regard to the quality of life of the elderly-was that the consumer price index as it applies to the elderly is really meaningless. It is not geared to the needs or the purchasing patterns of elderly people.
Why do I say that? I say it for two reasons. One of the reasons, I suggest, is the criteria on which the consumer price index is based, the population coverage or what is popularly called the target group. I think it is worth reading into the record. I am referring to the study of the consumer price index for Canada put out by Statistics Canada, catalogue No. 62-539. It reads:
The population group to which the CPI refers, commonly called the target group, delimits the specific segment of the population whose spending pattern is used to derive the relative importance of goods and services in the market basket. In selecting the target group, the objective was to secure wide representation or urban families with reasonably similarity in spending patterns among various groupings of family types and incomes.
Accordingly, the CPI population reference group for Canada has been updated in the present revisions according to the following criteria:
(a)	Those living in Canadian urban centres with metropolitan populations
exceeding 30,000;
Do our elderly fit into that pattern? Not badly. Some of them may be out in the country. It goes on to read:
(b)	Those ranging in size from two to six persons, consisting of any combination of adults or of adults and children.
I wonder if this really fits those about whom we are concerned at the moment. It goes on to read:
(c)	Those with annual incomes in 1967 ranging from $4,000 to $12,000.
Here is where we must depart from many of those who are eligible for pension settlements. I suggest that this is one reason why the target group aimed at by the consumer price index which is used for indexing pensions is not really helpful as it refers to the elderly.
But there is another reason, and that is the breakdown of buying patterns. It is an interesting buying pattern developed
Old Age Security Act
with great care. I do not criticize it on the grounds of the care with which it was developed for the purposes for which it is intended, but I maintain that it cannot be applied with any degree of credibility to those who are engaging our attention tonight.
Is as much beef being brought by our elderly as dairy products? We are told that 3.2 per cent of the basket is supposed to be beef and 3.3 per cent dairy products. I suggest that this is not quite in balance for the elderly. As much as 5.9 per cent is allowed on red meat as against .9 per cent on chicken and only .39 per cent on fish. I suggest that this pattern of buying fails if one were to examine the basket brought home by the elderly. It is obviously designed for persons with adequate incomes, to select according to taste and the need to provide bodily warmth and growth.
The sort of selecting I have seen among the elderly is one that is closely regulated by the price of the product offered. I have seen constituents of mine pick up a single pork chop and put it down because it is too expensive. They looked at the unit price and found that a pair of herring is much cheaper than a pork chop, so they will buy the herring. You will remember that at one time pork was a very popular item because it was cheap, and at another time it was chicken. I am not sure which item is cheap now for this particular type of buyer.
To go back to buying patterns generally, there is a suggestion that .9 per cent of the buying is for sirloin and only .8 per cent for hamburger. Surely even the buying in my own family does not respond to that particular proportion. For fruits and vegetables we have 3.2 per cent and for dairy products 3.3 per cent. I suggest that these figures may not be arbitrary, but they are not geared to the elderly.
On drinks such as tea, coffee and soft drinks, tea and coffee account for 3.5 per cent and soft drinks account for .7 per cent. This is ludicrous. These figures apply better to teenagers. Imagine allowing as much on pop as on tea!
Something I do not understand is 17.8 per cent on housing but only 8 per cent on rented premises and 9.48 per cent on home ownership. I do not understand this particular aspect of the price index anyway because it deals with both home ownership and rented premises. Surely it is one or the other. If you are going to have it as a component, they should be weighted the same but broken down internally. But who in this particular class is both a home owner and rents premises?
Do senior citizens spend about the same proportion of their expenditures on telephone services as on childrens clothing? It states here that it is 1.49 per cent as against 1.45 per cent. They must have an awful lot of grandchildren because they are either talking to them or buying clothing for them. They are allowed a little more than that on footwear, that is 1.58 per cent. The whole thing is ludicrous.
Transportation is another matter. Transportation counts for 15 per cent, when in most urban areas senior citizens travel free on the bus, or at half price, or at least at some discount, and not all senior citizens can afford a car, whereas this index provides 13 per cent for the purchase, operation and upkeep of the car.

My argument, therefore, is that indexing of pensions on the basis of a completely inapplicable consumer price index is deceptive and could be wrong. They could be diddled, they could be done out of what is their due. It is suggested that persons benefiting from that indexing are keeping pace in their purchasing with the items that are mentioned, when usually they buy in a completely different pattern in order to provide the sustenance of life.
The old age security and all the indexed pensions should therefore be adjusted in accordance with an index which measures very accurately the changes in the cost to those to whom the pension applies-the cost to the senior citizens for the expenditures they make, properly weighted for food as against housing, and properly weighted between tea, coffee and pop, and for clothing and transportation. Then and then only will justice be more nearly done. As matters stand now, great injustices are probably being perpetrated.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) has been considered by many people to be a Scrooge in many areas, but nowhere is he as much of a Scrooge as in dealing with services and pensions for the senior citizens of Canada.
This bill is supposedly designed to make old age security residence requirements a little better. I have some doubts about the proposed new rules and whether they will accomplish the corrective action required to treat our senior citizens in a more fair and equitable manner.
The bill deals with certain specific subjects. I think one of the most significant things about it is that it does not deal with certain subjects. A couple of years ago I wrote to the minister about a particular problem that is faced by widows, and I am sure he has received representations from other sources as well. There is in this country something known as a spouses allowance where a pension is paid to a spouse who reaches age 60 when the other spouse reaches age 65 and becomes pensionable. That was a progressive step. In most cases the one who reaches age 65 first is the male, who is normally considered to be the breadwinner. In the past he had the problem of retiring at age 65 and supporting his spouse, who is normally not working at that age, on the one pension.
The allowance was a step forward to provide relief to the man who wanted to retire, or to the woman who if she happened to be the breadwinner who wanted to retire and along with her spouse live off the old age pension and the guaranteed income supplement. There is also the situation of the widow whose husband had been eligible for old age pension and who now has no pension available to her. If the husband had not died, the woman would have drawn the pension at age 60, but now since she is a widow she gets no pension at all. In a letter to me the minister promised to bring in legislation to deal with this problem and I had hoped he would have taken advantage of the legislation before us to do so, but unfortunately that is not the case. I think he is to be severely castigated for that glaring omission.

Another aspect of old age pensions is the guaranteed income supplement. I can understand the theory behind it-that it is given only to those in greatest need or those who have no other source of income. I suppose there are two sides to the argument for supporting or not supporting that approach, but it strikes me as being rather unfair to senior citizens who have made provision for their old age and have struggled to save money for it. They are being penalized by not being eligible for the guaranteed income supplement. This is discouraging people from saving for their old age and has the effec. of increasing greater dependency on government handouts.
I would be inclined to suggest that the guaranteed income supplement should be reassessed to reward those who have been responsible and made provision for their old age to ensure they get whatever is available from the public purse on the same basis as those who had been less responsible or less fortunate. Perhaps the most glaring complaint is that the combined old age pension and guaranteed income supplement are too low.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PENSION PAYABLE TO PERSONS 65 YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext: I think we have enough senior citizens to represent the ratio of the population and others to represent other age groups and segments of Canadian life.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PENSION PAYABLE TO PERSONS 65 YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext: On that basis, there should be a lot more of us here.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PENSION PAYABLE TO PERSONS 65 YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext:
There should be a lot more of them particularly in this party, and not the one to my left which seems to have a preponderance of senior citizens.
I want to comment on the proposal the minister is putting forward. I think there is something wrong with a system in which an immigrant who becomes a Canadian citizen earns one fortieth of full pension per year only until age 65. On the surface it may sound fair enough, but what if this person is self-employed and continues to be an economically productive member of society until age 70 or 75? If he arrived in Canada at age 55 the most his pension could amount to would be ten
February 8, 1977

fortieths of the full pension because he would no longer qualify even if working after age 65. He might decide to defer applying for old age security beyond age 65 if he knew that by doing so he would be earning a larger share of the full pension when he stopped working. It seems to me it would be quite logical to introduce this kind of flexibility.
If an individual at age 65 felt strong and healthy, he should not be penalized for that but should be able to continue earning some "pension points", so to speak, so that when he stopped working he would be entitled to a slightly better pension than if he had stopped at age 65 as the present proposal assumes he would. Even if he did stop working at age 65 he might be just as productive as a man who had been collecting welfare or unemployment insurance almost from the day he came to Canada. These comments have been by way of preliminary introduction to the key issue I want to discuss. It has to do with the fact that the government has been negligent in areas in which more progress for the elderly in our society could be made.
In my view the government has been slow to develop other services for the elderly. For some strange reason, for the past couple of decades we have thought that you need only provide the elderly with a small pension and put them in an institution, and that would be enough. I take issue with that approach; it is not right. First, that approach is much too costly, and I think particularly of the cost of institutions. Second, the elderly do not want it. In my view, and I have talked with many elderly people, they would far prefer to stay in their own residence, if possible, or perhaps with their families, than be placed in an institution as soon as they reach retirement age.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PENSION PAYABLE TO PERSONS 65 YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext: They don't like being put out to pasture.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PENSION PAYABLE TO PERSONS 65 YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext:
Basically, we need to readjust our philosophy underlying the treatment of our senior citizens. Instead of giving them a little pension and putting them into an institution, we could perhaps give them a better pension and keep them at home a lot longer. As well, we ought to provide those services which will make it possible for them to stay home longer.
At present 8 per cent, or almost two million individuals, of the Canadian population consists of people 65 years old or more. By the turn of the century there will be approximately 3.4 million Canadians in this category. That figure represents a 250 per cent increase in the aged population at the turn of the century, as compared with an estimated total population increase of 75 per cent for the same period.
The elderly, it is clear, are now major users of the health care system and will become increasingly so in the future, as the proportion of the aged in our population increases. Hospital utilization, measured by patient days used by the elderly in general and allied special hospitals, will increase from 35 per cent in 1971 to over 42 per cent by the year 2001. Based on current practice, it is estimated that by the turn of the century we shall need an additional 166 hospitals, each with 300 beds,
Old Age Security Act
to accommodate the predicted increase in the aged population. The hospitals it is predicted we shall need will be provided at staggering cost. For this reason alone we ought to consider alternatives to institutions.
Canadians tend to resort to institutionalization more than is altogether necessary. If this trend could be reversed and the taxpayers saved the cost of these institutions, governments would be in a better position to increase old age pensions. The result would be that senior citizens could be more self-reliant, and would be better able to provide for their own care.
The Canadian Senate Committee on Aging estimated that, in the period 1962-63, 8.5 per cent of the Ontario population 65 and over was in some kind of institution on any one day, compared with less than 5 per cent in the United Kingdom. Clearly the province of Ontario puts a proportionately larger number into institutions than does the United Kingdom. More recently it was estimated that in 1972-73 9 per cent of the population of Ontario aged 65 and over was or is in an institution of some sort. As one can see, relevant figures rose from 8.5 per cent in 1962-63 to over 9 per cent in 1972-73. One reason for this rise, I suggest, is that there is little or no alternative to institutional care.
The provision of more beds is not a solution to the health problems of the elderly. In Winnipeg, between 1966 and 1974, while the population of those 65 years old and over increased by 17 per cent, the number of nursing home beds increased by 91 per cent. Some may think that these figures reflect to the credit of the government, something to be proud of; I suggest that the opposite is true. We should be ashamed of them.
The elderly also use non-institutional health services in greater measure than their share of the population would lead one to expect. According to 1971 figures, in Quebec 14.5 per cent of medical services rendered by doctors was for those 65 years old and over; 37 per cent of home visits was for persons 65 and over; the number of services per person aged 65 years and over was 11, compared with 4.8 for those under 65 years; the number of examinations per person 65 years and over was 6.9, compared with 2.9 for those under 65 years. It is therefore apparent that the increase in the aged population associated with the increase in utilization of health services will be one of the major problems in the health care field in the future. Moreover, I point out that most elderly Canadians wish to remain in their homes and communities; indeed, it is healthier to keep them there and much less costly.
The elderly have many health problems associated with their condition. They have diminished reserves, and the functions of various organs are altered. Their medical problems are complicated by the presence of multiple diseases, different presentation and response to disease and differing response to drug therapy. Also, the difficulty to ascertain disease is widespread, and nutritional deficiencies are common. That is to say, one finds among the elderly nutritional deficiencies which are not common to the general population. This perhaps shows that pensions are too low and senior citizens cannot afford to

February 8, 1977
Old Age Security Act
buy proper nourishment, or that we lack proper services with which to keep a close eye on senior citizens and make sure they are properly nourished and looked after. Senior citizens take longer to recover from disease, and treatment must be aimed more at overcoming disabilities and improving function than at obtaining absolute cure.
The elderly are subject to complicating social problems which include loneliness, isolation, financial difficulties, bereavement, loss of status, and poor accommodation, that is to say, poor shelter.
There has been little formal undergraduate education in geriatrics and gerontology in Canada, which highlights one of our important deficiencies in terms of our ability to care for senior citizens. The fact is that there are too few specialists in geriatrics in this country and not enough training facilities to train those who would work in the fields of geriatrics and gerontology in this country. This state of affairs reflects shamefully on the minister, who has been responsible for his present portfolio for a number of years, and on the government, which has been in power now some 14 or 15 years. If our people cannot change these conditions and correct the problems I have outlined, their only obvious alternative is to change the government which has resisted taking progressive action of the sort which other governments, of other countries, have taken, to show that they appreciate what those who built up their countries did.
The World Health Organization has recommended the initiation of geriatric services as a solution to the health problems of the aging. The aims of such preventive geriatric services should be to keep the elderly in their homes within the local community for as long as they are able and desire to remain there, and to train all those who work with the elderly in the special ways in which disease presents itself in the aged, and how to detect illness in the early stages.
Britain has six chairs of geriatric medicine. In Canada there is a well developed geriatric department at Deer Lodge Hospital in Winnipeg, and recently a demonstration model for a community geriatric service based at St. Boniface Hospital has been recommended.
In Ontario, apart from Sunnybrook, the University of Western Ontario has appointed a co-ordinator of geriatric care in the Department of Medicine; Queen's University has instituted a division of geriatric and continuing care medicine, and McMaster has a consultant gerontologist for the health science faculty. This represents only a very small segment of Canada's population that is being served.
I believe it would be useful to outline the services offered by the Sunnybrook Medical Centre in Toronto as a good example of a pattern that might be used in other places to establish services which are required, and to which I have been making reference in the past few minutes.
There is an assessment unit which assesses the mental and physical condition of an elderly patient. There is a rehabilitation unit which provides many forms of rehabilitation to people who require it. There is a psychiatric unit especially designed to deal with the special psychiatric problems which senior citizens face. They are different from those faced by Canadians in other age groups.
There are long term wards for those who must be kept there on a long-term basis. There are domiciliary and self-care units which provide service on a shorter term basis to people who require less attention by others.
They have a community care program which includes daytime admissions only, a day hospital. There is a home care program which provides various services to people while at home. This home care program is administered from the hospital. It follows up patients who have come and gone, providing services which enable them to remain at home and yet receive the appropriate care.
They have a geriatric assessment and consultation clinic as well as follow-up clinics. They also have a program of education of medical people. First year family practice residents rotate through the department for a couple of months at a time in order to increase the knowledge and ability of general practitioners to deal with special problems of the aged.
There are some particular proposals for further development of preventive geriatric services. Perhaps that kind of service could do more to ease the burden of life for senior citizens than many of the others. It would do a lot to ease the burden of costs for treating patients who have been neglected. They may come in with one kind of an illness or another which, if it had been dealt with earlier, could have been prevented.
Special in-patient units are being considered in an intermittent re-admission program. Under this program a patient is admitted for six weeks and returns home for six weeks. This pattern is continued on an alternating basis. It allows the patient to spend half of his time at home while providing his family with a six week break during which time his physical health can be brought to an optimal level while he is in hospital.
Essentially what you have here is one bed being used for two patients simultaneously but alternately. That is an obvious reduction in the cost of an institution. You have two patients being cared for out of one bed.
There is a proposal for a palliative care unit, something that does not exist in many places in this country. It should be established in many areas. Work in various institutions in various parts of the world has shown the value of these kinds of units. They deal with those who are terminally ill or in severe pain for which there is no cure. They require hospitalization measures to ease the pain or to be ensured greater comfort during their last few days or weeks. This is something which governments throughout this country should examine.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
(Mr. Yewchuk.]

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-SUGGESTED REDUCTION TO 60 OF ELIGIBLE AGE FOR RETIREMENT TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT FOR YOUNG PEOPLE
SOCIAL SECURITY-SUGGESTED REDUCTION TO 60 OF ELIGIBLE AGE FOR RETIREMENT TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT FOR YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not have many opportunities to rise in the adjournment debate.

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-SUGGESTED REDUCTION TO 60 OF ELIGIBLE AGE FOR RETIREMENT TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT FOR YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: Welcome!

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-SUGGESTED REDUCTION TO 60 OF ELIGIBLE AGE FOR RETIREMENT TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT FOR YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
Thank you. Since I feel the question I raised with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) on February 2 is extremely important but the minister did not share this view, I thought I should clarify the matter and urge the minister to reconsider his answer.
Be that as it may, I asked the minister whether he would suggest to his cabinet colleagues that the eligible age for voluntary retirement be reduced to 60 in order that those who so wish could retire from the labour market and provide jobs for a number of other people. In answer, the minister indicated that according to studies prepared by him or by others such a move would not create that many jobs. It would be preferable if the minister told the House which agencies prepared those studies and stated their findings so the House could peruse them.
It is quite evident that, assuming we had a plant employing 100 people and 20 workers retired voluntarily to receive voluntary retirement pension at 60, there would be no job openings if the employer forced the 80 remaining workers to increase their effort and put out the same volume of production. Such however would be an exceptional case, and the labour unions would see to it that things back were put back in order, to end the agony of remaining workers.
Personally, Mr. Speaker, I know a great many people between 60 and 65 who would be anxious to retire for various reasons. They would like to be able to travel when they are still physically fit to do so and they tell me it is much nicer to travel when both spouses are in good physical condition. It would be more pleasant to travel and to enjoy the few good years of their life.
There are 896,000 persons of both sexes between 60 and 65, and it is believed that at least 40 per cent of them, or 358,000, belong to the labour force. Let us suppose that 50 per cent of them would volunteer to retire, this would mean 179,000 job openings. If these were filled by young people between 19 and
Adjournment Debate
30 years of age, we would hope that a number of them who wish to get married would be able to realize their dream. At least it would help them do so and they might even wish to buy their own house. Eventually, this would stimulate the building trades and give jobs to the workers of this industry.
For my part, Mr. Speaker, I believe that our society would stand to gain if we were to facilitate the access of young people to the labour market. This could also contribute to increasing the birth rate to ensure a natural and normal growth in the Canadian population. All those reasons favour lowering the age for voluntary retirement to 60. For the good of older people, they should be allowed to spend their energy in doing something worthwhile, because otherwise, if they are not given this opportunity-and they say that idleness is the root of all evil-they will do something else.
For my part, I know very well that it would not have been a good thing to let me spend too long with nothing to do when I was very young. I would have found ways to use up my energies. When we get older and more mature and have gained much experience of life, we can remain idle with not much danger, and society will not be any the worse for it. This is another advantage that we must consider. I know many people of 60, 62 or 64 who live comfortably and who have already retired. They take better care of their property because they have more time than when they had to go to work. This improves their environment and encourages the young people to better appreciate their environment and their country. This is another factor that we must consider. Many of those people grow a garden and this shows the young people that the earth has some use and that we must take advantage of it.
There are also people who do odd jobs, who do all kinds of things to keep busy, useful things for their neighbourhood and their family. I know some of these people who belong to golden age clubs. I congratulate the minister for implementing the New Horizons program. These are properly managed funds.
For all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I urge again the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) to reconsider this matter and these suggestions from hon. members in order to put forward as soon as possible a legislation which would allow people to retire when they are 60 on a voluntary basis, and I emphasize the word "voluntary".

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-SUGGESTED REDUCTION TO 60 OF ELIGIBLE AGE FOR RETIREMENT TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT FOR YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is very difficult within a three minute time limit to answer the various arguments put forward by the hon. member, who speaks with so much conviction and sincerity.
The problem he raises I think is of concern to many members and citizens in this country. Unhappily, the points he made, although valid in many respects, contain as well other aspects on which he did not have time to elaborate and which I will not be able to cover either within the short time at my disposal. For instance, he speaks about voluntary retirement. I simply wish to ask him what will he do about spouses at home? A woman who has worked in her home, who has brought up a family during all her life, would be as much entitled as her
80008-44Vi

February 8, 1977
Adjournment Debate
husband who has worked in a plant, on a farm or elsewhere, to say she wants voluntary retirement at 60. And I do not see how, when he talked about some 900,000 people, he could cut that figure in half by saying half of them are working and then again cutting it in half when he added maybe half of that half will want to retire. I regret but he left out the 450,000 spouses who would not hesitate to ask for benefits, and rightly so, if ever such an idea were carried out and people started to demand early retirement under the old age security program in those terms...

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-SUGGESTED REDUCTION TO 60 OF ELIGIBLE AGE FOR RETIREMENT TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT FOR YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: Man and wife!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-SUGGESTED REDUCTION TO 60 OF ELIGIBLE AGE FOR RETIREMENT TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT FOR YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
The hon. member says man and wife. So right then the figures he mentioned should be twice what he had forecast. I would probably say more than twice those figures. Our computation was made within the department. It shows that if all people between 60 and 65 could benefit from that program, it would cost us more than $2 billion in 1977, supposing that only one half of that total figure-and, once again, we should take the spouses into account-would benefit from early retirement. So we would already have more than an additional $1 billion in outlays.
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes I have left, I would like to raise the problem of those who find it too soon to retire at 65 and who would like to go on working, to have a job. They protest because, in many cases, in their factories they are obliged to retire at 65. This is something new, due mainly to an increased life expectancy and we can see this phenomenon in various countries, particularly in the Scandinavian countries and also in the United States. New pressures are brought to bear that people can have the right to work after 65. As we can see, many people are concerned by this problem but, unfortunately, I do not think that we can seriously deal with it tonight. However, I would be pleased to discuss it with the hon. member on another occasion.

subtopic: CUSTOMS-PURCHASING OF GROCERIES IN UNITED STATES BY RESIDENTS OF BRITISH COLUMBIA-GOVERNMENT ACTION
CUSTOMS-PURCHASING OF GROCERIES IN UNITED STATES BY RESIDENTS OF BRITISH COLUMBIA-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 15 last I asked the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin) a question regarding the shopping practices of Canadians in British Columbia, for example, why they go south of the border to Bellingham, Washington, to do their shopping. First of all I want to make it clear that I am thankful for some of the work that the minister has done. She is the first minister in that department, among the parade of three or four ministers that we have already had over the last three or four years, who is doing something for the customs officers in that area. One thing she has done is to add four more man-years to the present staff there on a casual basis.
I should just like to interject at this point that although these man-years are casual at the present time, they ought to be permanent man-years. I say this because the traffic is going to increase and the staff at the customs post are already
overworked. Therefore I ask the minister to reconsider the present casual classification of the men working there and to place them on a permanent basis.
The minister herself wondered why people shop south of the border. I do not go grocery shopping very often, but when I do I am shocked at the way the price of food commodities goes up every time. I certainly do not go shopping in the United States. I am not an authority on this, so I went to the best Canadian authority on the price of groceries there is, the ordinary housewife.
I went to a young mother with three children who does her shopping in the United States because she saves money by going there. I learned that she saves $20 every two weeks, which is something like $40 a month. That is nothing to sneeze at when you are trying to raise a young family. I would like to tell the House about the things she buys there, and the amount she saves by doing so.
The American price of Sugar Crisp, a cereal, is $1.02 and the Canadian price is $1.51, 50 per cent higher in Canada. Rolled oats, good Canadian food, costs 98 cents in the United States and $1.13 in Canada. Frosted flakes cost $1.01 in the United States and $1.30 in Canada. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is always bragging about what a great thing he is doing for Canadian farmers, but here is the way it turns out with regard to the price of corn. In the United States corn costs 28 cents per tin, and in Canada it is 51 cents a tin.
A shopper in the United States pays $1.68 for six tins of corn, and in Canada that shopper pays $3.06. Beans cost 24 cents in the United States and 41 cents in Canada. If four cans are bought in the United States, the cost is 96 cents, and in Canada the cost is $1.64. Weiners cost 48 cents in the United States and 89 cents in Canada, and we wonder why shoppers go south of the border. The Canadian price is double that of the United States. The price of bacon in the United States is 89 cents, and in Canada it is 99 cents. Cheese in the United States costs 89 cents and in Canada $1.27.

subtopic: CUSTOMS-PURCHASING OF GROCERIES IN UNITED STATES BY RESIDENTS OF BRITISH COLUMBIA-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: How about cars?

subtopic: CUSTOMS-PURCHASING OF GROCERIES IN UNITED STATES BY RESIDENTS OF BRITISH COLUMBIA-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Cars are cheaper by a long shot. Ham costs 82 cents in the United States and 97 cents in Canada. Meat pies-packaged food-cost 24 cents in the United States and 38 cents in Canada. Let us consider one more item, tuna fish; it costs 44 cents in the United States and 71 cents in Canada. If a shopper buys four tins, he pays $1.76 in the United States and $2.84 in Canada.
The crowning example is Dare cookies, and the bag says "Head Office, Kitchener, Ontario". There is a plant in Surrey-White Rock, 20 miles from the border. As a matter of fact, that plant is 40 or 50 miles from Bellingham, where the shopping is done. Dare cookies cost 88 cents in the United States and $1.09 in Canada, where they are made. Pray tell, is there somebody on the government benches who can tell me why a Canadian product, made of Canadian agricultural
[Mr. Lalonde.)
February 8, 1977

products, costs more in Canada than it does when it is shipped across the border to the United States? I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) that question a week ago, but I received no answer.
Some may say that it does not pay to go across the border to shop because there is gas and wear and tear to be paid for, but gas is 10 cents or 12 cents a gallon cheaper there. People go down with an empty tank, fill it up there and save money on gas. It is one thing for a couple to raise a young family with the prices we have in Canada. They have a hard enough time, but what is it for people on fixed incomes who get, for example, $3 added to their pensions every three months because of the cost-of-living index? Is it any wonder that they pool their resources and go to the United States? We may think they are being disloyal to Canada, but all they are doing is trying to keep body and soul together. I would like to have an answer from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Baker (Gander-Twillingate)) as to why it is we have this kind of price differential.
The minister was a little catty in her answer when she said "I am anxious to hear his exact views as to what he wishes us to do". Pray tell, that is not my job. If the minister and the rest of her colleagues want to move over, we would gladly take that mandate and offer a few alternatives to the Canadian people. It is her job to look at the mess in which the government has put the country, and to give us the kind of economic policies that would deal with rising prices, prices that prevent people from being able to afford to shop in our own stores and buy
Adjournment Debate
our own products. It is cheaper to buy our own products in the United States. I am awaiting the reply of the parliamentary secretary on this.

speakeroldname: Mr. George Baker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: CUSTOMS-PURCHASING OF GROCERIES IN UNITED STATES BY RESIDENTS OF BRITISH COLUMBIA-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly want to thank the hon. gentleman and concur in his remarks about our excellent minister. I also want to thank him for his rundown of all the cheap prices in the United States. However, I think his question is misdirected when he asks it of this department. We have nothing to do with setting prices in the United States or with setting customs tariffs. Setting customs tariffs is the responsibility of the Department of Finance.
We have brought the matter of the tariffs to the attention of the Department of Finance. The hon. gentleman knowns that; he was told that in writing as well as in this House. Our position is that we do not attempt either to encourage or discourage grocery shopping in the United States because we cannot, but as a department of the government we do not want to act in a way to harm Canadian businessmen, manufacturers or producers.
